title: Deep Beneath Australia, Hidden Caves Could Reveal Secrets of Alien Worlds
content:
Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone creating a Swiss-cheese landscape where caves reach the surface. Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
Subtle trenches on the Nullarbor Plain reveal buried caves slowly collapsing upward, offering clues for finding other hidden cave systems.
Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient
shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago
Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant
barrier for plants, animals
, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “
the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams
In contrast,
the Mirning People
of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have
lived for tens of thousands of years
on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change, and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago.
Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
To an untrained eye, the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world.
Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground.
Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood
, partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface.
Our new study,
Communications Earth & Environment
, reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet.
The Bunda Cliffs mark the dramatic edge of the expansive, flat Nullarbor Plain where the arid limestone plains tumble to the Great Australian Bight. Distinct limestone layers are visible in the cliffs with the Nullarbor Limestone overlying the white, chalkier layer known as the Wilson Bluff Limestone. Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
Valleys, but not from rivers
Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions.
But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few metres) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models.
These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor.
They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water.
To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques.
A dirt track on the Nullarbor follows one of the long, almost imperceptible, shallow, north-south sediment-filled valleys. Greyer areas on the left of the foreground represent limestone at the surface. Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves.
Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside.
The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes.
This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface.
The results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It shows that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think.
One of the field team abseils into a collapse feature to record the sediment and reach the underyling cave system to measure the thickness and any disturbance of the geology. Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
Finding caves could help protect groundwater
Understanding where voids may exist underground can be important for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works,
mitigating geological hazards
, and accessing and protecting groundwater resources.
Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and
supply water to 10–25% of the global population
More fundamentally, caves are
important scientific archives
. Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time.
Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have
evolved and adapted in isolation
. These are some of the
least studied organisms on Earth
To learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard.
The dramatic Abrakurrie Cave system beneath the Nullarbor Plain. Photo shows the scale dwarfing the team member, as well as evidence of the cave collapse processes (pile of boulders and rubble in view) that allow the cave to move upwards through the overlying rocks to the surface over time. Credit: Field team archive GIAM ZRC SAZU
Clues for finding caves on Mars
The implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide
promising exploration sites for life on other planets
Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves,
including some thought to be related to karst on Mars
The Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be
attractive bases for future human explorers
How many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too.
Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand.
Reference: “Subdued surface expression of deep cave collapse” by Matej Lipar, Matthias Leopold, John A. Webb, Rok Ciglič, Jure Tičar, Matija Zorn, Uroš Stepišnik, Matej Jelovčan, Milo Barham, Matej Dolenec, Primož Miklavc, Tomislav Popit, Andrej Šmuc, Jian-xin Zhao and Mateja Ferk, 17 September 2026,
Communications Earth & Environment
DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-04016-7

title: He Was Looking for a Campsite. He Found a Massive Impact Crater
content:
The subtle circular shape of the Uhackatik impact structure in Quebec, with Lake Marsal near the center, is visible in this image captured on October 12, 2025, by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin
A camping search on satellite maps led to the discovery of a massive 390-million-year-old impact crater hidden in the Quebec wilderness.
An amateur astronomer searching satellite imagery for possible camping spots in Quebec ended up noticing something far more unusual: a previously unrecognized impact crater.
Only about 200 impact structures have been confirmed worldwide, although geologists believe
hundreds more may still be waiting to be found
. One of the newest additions to the
confirmed bin
is also a substantial one, and its discovery began with an amateur astronomer preparing for a camping trip.
A Strange Circle on a Satellite Map
In 2024, Joël Lapointe was looking over online maps while planning a trip to Quebec’s remote Côte Nord region when a circular feature near Lake Marsal caught his attention. He wondered whether the depression might have been created by an impact and reached out to specialists in Europe and North America.
That inquiry eventually prompted French researchers to
identify the lake area
at a 2024 meeting of the Meteoritical Society as the possible center of Quebec’s 11th known impact structure. The lead eventually reached Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University who directs the
Impact Earth
database.
At first, Osinski was doubtful. Still, the possibility was intriguing enough that he organized an expedition to the isolated location in October 2025.
Researchers arrive by floatplane on Lake Marsal to study the impact crater in October 2025. Credit: Gordon Osinski/Western University
Reaching the Crater Was a Challenge
Osinski and his colleagues traveled to the area by floatplane, but even getting onto land proved difficult. The aircraft was unable to reach the shoreline, forcing the team to carry their equipment through 50 meters (165 feet) of water.
Conditions did not improve once they reached solid ground. The landscape was swampy, rough, filled with insects, and covered in what Osinski called “deep, twisty, gnarly vegetation.” Although he had previously conducted fieldwork on six continents, he said this was among the toughest environments he had encountered.
Earlier geological surveys had interpreted the local breccia rocks as evidence of a diatreme, a funnel-shaped volcanic structure produced when explosive magma fragments surrounding rock.
“It’s the only unequivocal evidence of an impact event that you can see in the field with the naked eye,” Osinski said.
A 25 Kilometer Scar From an Ancient Collision
The object responsible for the impact was powerful enough to produce a complex crater structure measuring 25 kilometers (16 miles) across. The crater includes a central uplift as well as high cliffs displaying columnar jointing.
An impact of comparable magnitude in Quebec today would be catastrophic. Osinski said it would cause “regional devastation on a scale that would wipe out major cities and have global climate impacts.”
Analysis of collected rocks suggests the crater formed roughly 390 million years ago. That places the event about 100 million years before a
major increase in impact cratering
on Earth that researchers have suggested could be connected to collisions within the asteroid belt.
A panorama from the crater rim shows the varied terrain, trees, and lakes within the impact structure. Credit: Gordon Osinski/Western University
The Newly Named Uhackatik Crater
Following discussions with the Innu Council of Ekuanitshit, the researchers are calling the newly identified structure Uhackatik.
The team regards its impact origin as essentially confirmed, although a Meteoritical Society committee is expected to formally recognize the structure when it next convenes.
Uhackatik is the largest impact crater discovered since the 31-kilometer Hiawatha structure was identified in 2018.
Osinski is also part of NASA’s first Artemis Geology Team and helps train astronauts in geology. Even so, he does not expect Uhackatik to become an astronaut training destination anytime soon because reaching it is so difficult.
A younger and much more accessible impact site exists in Labrador, Kameshtashtan (also called Mistastin Lake), where astronauts have previously completed
geology training in the past
, he said.
An Amateur Observation Leads to a Major Find
For Lapointe, seeing his initial observation develop into a confirmed scientific discovery was unforgettable. He told
CityNews
that he was “over the Moon” when researchers determined that the structure really was an impact crater.
“I encourage everyone to not ignore intuition or an observation, even if it isn’t part of your field of expertise,” he told
another outlet
The discovery also shows how members of the public can contribute to scientific research. NASA offers
plenty of opportunities
for people interested in citizen science.
Through the
Daily Minor Planet project
, participants can search for asteroids and comets that could potentially threaten Earth. The Impact Flash project asks volunteers to examine dark regions of the Moon for brief flashes produced by meteoroid strikes. Meanwhile,
Exoasteroids
lets participants search for evidence of asteroids beyond our Solar System.

title: Anak Krakatau Just Blasted Ash 50,000 Feet Into the Sky
content:
Anak Krakatau erupts ash and volcanic gases in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 on September 5, 2026. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
Anak Krakatau blasted ash nearly 10 miles high, disrupting thousands of flights and sending a vast plume across Indonesia.
A powerful eruption from Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano sent ash high into the atmosphere, disrupting thousands of flights and worsening air quality.
Anak Krakatau, a small but highly active volcano located between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, erupts frequently. Most of its activity is relatively modest, but stronger episodes can create significant hazards. In early September 2026, the volcano produced a powerful eruption that continued for more than 24 hours, sending large amounts of gas and ash into the atmosphere. The event disrupted thousands of flights and reduced air quality in several parts of Indonesia, including Jakarta.
Satellites Capture Anak Krakatau’s Eruption
Satellites passing over the region on September 5 documented the eruption from above. The image shown above was captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite. It shows a white plume of volcanic gas rising above a brown cloud of ash.
A broader view from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) aboard the Suomi NPP satellite (below) reveals how widely the volcanic material spread across the surrounding region.
Plumes of ash and volcanic gases from Anak Krakatau drift over Indonesia and the Indian Ocean in this image captured by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on September 5, 2026. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
Ash Reaches 50,000 Feet
The ash posed a serious hazard to aviation, leading authorities to temporarily
close eight airports
on Java and Sumatra. According to
news reports
, nearly 3,000 flights traveling into and out of the region were disrupted.
Volcanic Ash Affects Jakarta and West Java
Ashfall also reached populated areas, particularly east of Anak Krakatau in Jakarta and other parts of West Java,
according to
the Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform (IHCP).
Volcanic ash can pose health risks because fine particles may irritate the respiratory tract, eyes, and skin. The IHCP noted, however, that the hazards associated with volcanic ash differ from those caused by
smoke produced by peatland fires
elsewhere in Indonesia. The two hazards differ in their particle properties, how they spread through the atmosphere, and the protective measures recommended for people exposed to them.
Anak Krakatau Continues to Rumble
The continuous explosive phase of the eruption eased on September 6, although Anak Krakatau remained active. The volcano shifted back toward its more typical pattern of
Strombolian eruptions
, which produce intermittent bursts of ash and other volcanic material.
Airports had
resumed operation
since early July

title: Surprising Diabetes Study Finds Tighter Blood Sugar Control May Come With a Hidden Cost
content:
Continuous glucose monitoring revealed a surprising connection between blood sugar patterns and next-day quality of life. The results suggest that well-being may depend on more than simply keeping glucose as steady as possible. Credit: Stock
People with diabetes felt better after days when their blood sugar had more room to fluctuate, suggesting that tighter control may sometimes come at the expense of daily life.
New research involving people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes found that spending more time within the normal glucose range predicted better quality of life the following day. Surprisingly, greater glucose fluctuations were also associated with improved well-being, suggesting that overly strict control may impose restrictions that interfere with everyday activities.
The research will be presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy (September 28 – October 2). It was led by Professor Dominic Ehrmann of FIDAM (Research Institute Diabetes Academy Mergentheim) in Bad Mergentheim, Germany.
Looking Beyond Glucose Targets
Preventing dangerously high or low blood sugar remains essential, but modern diabetes care also recognizes the mental effort required to make constant decisions about food, insulin, exercise, sleep, and daily routines. A treatment strategy that produces impressive numbers can still be difficult to sustain if it places too many limits on everyday life.
To explore that balance, the researchers examined whether glucose patterns recorded by continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices could predict how participants felt the following day. Unlike a single blood test, CGM tracks glucose around the clock and reveals how much time a person spends within, above, or below specific ranges.
The analysis was part of the PRO-MENTAL study, funded by the German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD). Participants rated their quality of life every day for 14 consecutive days using ecological momentary assessment (EMA), which captures experiences as they occur rather than asking people to recall them weeks or months later.
Tracking Daily Well-Being
Quality of life was measured with five statements adapted from the WHO-5 questionnaire:
I have felt cheerful and in good spirits
I have felt calm and relaxed
I have felt active and vigorous
I woke up feeling fresh and rested
My daily life has been filled with things that interest me
Participants also recorded their sleep quality, perceived stress, mood, and energy each day using the same EMA approach. Energy was rated on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 10 (very much).
The researchers matched those responses with CGM data collected during the same 14-day period. They calculated time below the safe range (TBR: <70 mg/dl), time above the safe range (TAR: >180 mg/dl), time in the normal range (normoglycemia) (TING: 70-140 mg/dl), and overall glucose variability.
Comparing Glucose With The Following Day
Statistical models tested whether glucose readings, sleep, stress, mood, and energy on one day predicted quality of life the next day. A separate analysis examined whether those factors were connected to quality of life on the same day.
The calculations accounted for age, sex, diabetes type, and each participant’s previous quality of life score. This helped the researchers determine whether the observed relationships persisted beyond a person’s usual level of well-being.
The study included 400 people with diabetes. Of those participants, 72% had type 1 diabetes, 28% had type 2 diabetes, and 55% were female. Their median age was 47 years (range 32-63 years), and their average glycated hemoglobin level (HbA1c – a measure of blood sugar control) was 7.6%.
More Time In Range Predicted Better Days
People who spent more time within the normal glucose range on one day tended to report better quality of life the next day. Time spent above or below the safe range, however, was not significantly associated with next-day quality of life.
The more surprising result involved glucose variability. Participants also reported better quality of life after days when their glucose varied more than usual. Glucose measurements recorded on the same day did not show a significant relationship with that day’s quality of life.
Sleep and energy mattered as well. Better sleep during the previous night and feeling more energetic on the preceding day were both associated with improved quality of life, showing that glucose was only one part of the broader picture.
The Cost Of Pursuing Perfect Control
The authors said: “Days with higher time in the normal safe range for blood sugar were followed by days on which individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes reported better quality of life, underscoring the importance of optimal blood sugar control for well-being.
“Interestingly, higher-than-usual glucose variability was also associated with improved next-day quality of life. These findings may suggest that individuals experience lower quality of life when attempting to minimize glucose fluctuations too strictly, potentially due to the associated burden or restrictions in daily life, which may contribute to some people living with diabetes feeling unable to safely engage in certain activities.”
Meeting: Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD)

title: Just 5% of Pancreatic Cancer Cells Can Shield an Entire Tumor From Immune Attack
content:
Pancreatic tumors may exploit a biological pathway normally involved in clotting and wound repair to evade immune attack. Credit: Stock
A tiny faction of pancreatic cancer cells can turn its surroundings into an immune-safe zone, protecting neighboring tumor cells along with itself.
Researchers at the
Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
have uncovered how rare groups of pancreatic cancer cells reshape their immediate surroundings to keep immune cells away. Disrupting these localized defenses slowed tumor growth and helped immunotherapy work more effectively in preclinical models, revealing a possible way to weaken one of cancer’s most stubborn forms.
The findings, published in
, center on fibrin, a mesh-forming protein best known for helping blood clots and wounds heal. Certain pancreatic cancer cells appear to exploit this repair system, stabilizing fibrin around themselves and creating protected neighborhoods that shelter nearby cancer cells as well.
How Pancreatic Tumors Shut Out Immune Cells
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a five-year survival rate of about 13 percent. While immunotherapies have transformed the treatment of several cancers, most pancreatic tumors remain resistant. Their dense surroundings contain scar-like tissue and immune-suppressing cells that can block T cells from reaching malignant cells or leave the T cells too exhausted to attack.
“Pancreatic cancer has remained one of the most difficult cancers to treat because it is exceptionally good at shielding itself from the immune system,” said Brian D. Brown, PhD, Mount Sinai Professor of Genetic Engineering, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and senior author of the study. “We found that a surprisingly small population of cancer cells can organize local environments that suppress immune responses and protect not only themselves but neighboring cancer cells as well. If we can disrupt these protective niches, we may be able to make immunotherapy more effective for patients.”
To examine how different cancer cell populations influence their surroundings, the researchers used Perturb-map, a spatial genomics platform developed at Mount Sinai. The technology combines gene editing, molecular barcodes, and detailed imaging to show where genetically distinct tumor cells grow and which immune cells gather around them. This allowed the team to study the cellular diversity found within tumors rather than treating every cancer cell as biologically identical.
The analysis showed that cancer cells begin reorganizing their local immune neighborhoods before particular clones become dominant. This suggests that some cells gain an advantage not simply by growing faster, but by changing the environment around them in ways that help them survive.
Two Proteins Build A Fibrin Barrier
Two proteins emerged as major organizers of these protected areas: PAI1 and PAI2. Both interfere with enzymes that normally help break down fibrin. By slowing that removal process, the proteins allow a fibrin-rich framework to accumulate around the cancer cells.
That framework attracts and retains macrophages, immune cells that can either support or restrain inflammation depending on the signals they receive. Inside these tumor niches, the macrophages adopt immune-suppressing behavior and help exclude cancer-killing T cells.
The discovery may also illuminate pancreatic cancer’s connection to dangerous blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis. The same pathway that preserves fibrin around a tumor could contribute to excessive clotting elsewhere, linking immune escape with a well-known complication of the disease.
A Few Cells Reshape The Whole Neighborhood
In laboratory models, a population containing only 5 percent PAI1-producing pancreatic cancer cells was enough to increase immune-suppressing macrophages and reduce activated T cells nearby. The protection extended beyond the cells producing the protein to neighboring cancer cells.
“We discovered that immune suppression isn’t spread evenly throughout a pancreatic tumor,” said Chiara Falcomatà, PhD, postdoctoral fellow at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and first author of the study. “Instead, small groups of cancer cells create localized neighborhoods that protect themselves and nearby cancer cells from immune attack. Understanding how these protective niches form gives us new opportunities to target them therapeutically.”
When the researchers deleted the genes responsible for PAI1 or PAI2, tumor burden in mice fell by more than half. The altered tumors contained more than twice as many CD8 T cells, along with substantially more activated cancer-killing T cells and fewer terminally exhausted ones.
Dismantling the Tumor’s Defenses
Removing either gene also made pancreatic tumors more responsive to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, a treatment designed to release a molecular brake on T cells. In one mouse experiment, combining anti-PD-1 treatment with the loss of PAI1 or PAI2 nearly doubled median survival from 24 to 47 days.
The team then tested PAI-039, an experimental drug that inhibits PAI1. Combining the drug with anti-PD-1 therapy extended survival in two pancreatic cancer models, even though anti-PD-1 treatment produced little benefit on its own. Blocking the interaction between fibrin and macrophages yielded similar results, suggesting that the pathway could be interrupted at several points.
A Pathway With Potential Beyond Cancer
“Our findings suggest there may be several opportunities to interrupt this pathway,” Dr. Brown said. “Whether by targeting the proteins produced by cancer cells, the fibrin-rich environment they create, or the immune cells recruited into these regions, each approach offers a potential strategy for making pancreatic tumors more vulnerable to immune attack.”
“Our findings also add to a growing understanding of the connection between the clotting system, wound healing, and macrophage control in many different diseases and even aging,” added Dr. Brown. “This goes beyond cancer. PAI1 levels have a very strong association with aging, and a similar fibrin-macrophage axis has been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease. Developing ways to target this axis may have broad therapeutic applications.”
The study combined several preclinical models with spatial transcriptomics and imaging of patient tumors. Those human samples revealed similar immune-suppressing niches around rare pancreatic cancer cells expressing the genes for PAI1 and PAI2, but the treatment experiments were conducted in animals. Further research must determine whether dismantling these niches can be done safely and effectively in people.
Reference: “A serpin–myeloid axis in pancreatic cancer heterogeneity and immune evasion” by Chiara Falcomatà, Maximilian M. Schaefer, Bhavya Singh, Divya Chhamalwan, Alexander Tepper, Sebastian R. Nielsen, Hunter T. Potak, Maxime Dhainaut, Gurkan Mollaoglu, Matthew D. Park, Miriam Merad, Alessia Baccarini and Brian D. Brown, 9 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11002-8

title: Alzheimer’s Brain Damage May Begin Outside the Brain
content:
Scientists traced a damaging immune response in tau-related neurodegeneration to signals originating in the body’s lymph nodes. In mice, disrupting this pathway protected neurons and cognition even though toxic tau tangles remained in the brain. Credit: Stock
A study found that immune cells that drive neurodegeneration, the progressive damage and loss of nerve cells, originate in the body’s lymph nodes.
In mice whose brains accumulate clumps of tau protein, researchers found a way to protect nerve cells without clearing away those clumps. They interrupted an immune response directed from outside the brain, where lymph nodes give instructions to T cells, immune cells that normally help defend the body.
Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis
team found that blocking those instructions from birth protected the mice against brain damage and preserved their cognitive abilities. The results point to a possible treatment strategy for Alzheimer’s disease and related tau disorders that targets immune activity beyond the brain itself.
The study was published in
Nature Neuroscience
. Along with Alzheimer’s, tau accumulates in a group of disorders called primary tauopathies. Whether the approach can protect against damage when started later in life is still being investigated.
A target beyond the blood-brain barrier
Targeting cells outside the brain could help researchers avoid a major obstacle in drug development. The blood-brain barrier, a tightly controlled boundary between the bloodstream and brain tissue, limits the entry of many substances, including medicines.
“One of the issues in developing treatments for neurological diseases is that you need to engineer your treatment so that it gets into the brain and past the blood-brain barrier, but we might not actually need to get the drugs into the central nervous system to mitigate neurodegeneration,” said senior author David M. Holtzman, MD, the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine’s Department of Neurology. “There are lots of ways to manipulate T cells that have been studied extensively and that are approved treatments for other diseases, but many haven’t yet been explored for neurodegenerative diseases.”
WashU Medicine researchers have found that blocking immune cells in the body’s lymph nodes significantly reduces Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration in mice. Shown are a mouse brain with tissue damage typical of Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration (left) and a brain in which the harmful immune response was prevented (right). Credit: Hao Hu
Tracing the cells that instruct T cells
The brains of people with Alzheimer’s and related disorders contain far more T cells than healthy brains. In a
previous study
, Holtzman’s team found that eliminating T cells in the brain prevented much of the nerve cell damage in mice modeling the effects of tau accumulation. That left unanswered where the T cells came from and what directed them to the brain.
Certain T cells rely on another type of immune cell, called a dendritic cell, to identify molecular targets for attack. The researchers focused on classical dendritic cells type 1, or cDC1. Very few of these cells reside in the brain, and those present did not appear to interact with the T cells that accumulated after tau tangles developed. The cells giving the instructions therefore seemed likely to be elsewhere.
The team included first author Hao Hu, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow, and co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology. Working with collaborators, they eliminated dendritic cells from lymph nodes and other locations in mice that ordinarily develop tau tangles and neurodegeneration.
Without those dendritic cells, the usual rise in brain T cells, particularly a subset called CD8 T cells, disappeared, along with the associated brain damage. The mice retained their cognitive abilities despite unchanged levels of tau tangles. These results suggest that interrupting T cell activity may help slow or reduce cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer’s, although the demonstrated protection was in mice.
The immune trigger remains unknown
What initially prompts the dendritic cells to activate T cells remains unknown. Holtzman suspects that tau-related damage releases material from brain cells that then travels to lymph nodes in the neck. Dendritic cells may identify that material as something T cells should attack.
“Until not that long ago, most people, including myself, did not think that the immune response was even involved in neurodegenerative diseases that are due to protein accumulation in the brain,” Holtzman said. “That these dendritic cells are involved in neurodegenerative disease is exciting; we’ve shown they’re important, and that they are a potential target for future therapy.”
His team is now testing whether disrupting dendritic cell function in midlife, around the onset of tau tangles, can provide the same protection as blocking it from birth. The researchers are also trying to identify the specific signal that guides T cells to the brain so they can explore ways to block it.
Reference: “Priming of CD8+ T cells by peripheral dendritic cells exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration” by Hao Hu, Peter Bor-Chian Lin, Carisa Zeng, Yongyi Li, Megan E. Bosch, Joshua T. Emmerson, Prabal Sharma, Ray A. Ohara, Wendy Dong, Tong Wu, Siling Du, Wenqing Gao, Hong Jiang, Liya Yuan, Xin Bao, Shasha Li, Anthony N. title: Physicists Tackle a Classic Quantum Problem With a Powerful New Computational Method
content:
An AI-generated illustration depicting the Kondo effect. Conducting electrons in a metal are shown interacting with the spin of an embedded magnetic atom impurity. Credit: AI-generated artwork by Linqing Peng
A new computational approach uses the real electronic structure of materials to predict a classic quantum effect far more accurately than simplified models.
Seven magnetic atoms embedded one at a time in copper have given physicists a new way to test whether computers can predict the behavior of real quantum materials without first reducing them to simplified models.
For most of the seven transition-metal impurities, calculations developed by researchers at Caltech and Yale University improved on the accuracy of conventional model-based predictions by as much as two orders of magnitude. The test involved the Kondo effect, a classic quantum problem whose general physics has been understood for decades even though its precise behavior in specific materials has remained difficult to calculate.
That gap between understanding the physics and predicting a real material is what the researchers set out to close. Rather than simplifying the electronic structure of the material before calculating its behavior, the team adapted highly accurate computational techniques originally developed in quantum chemistry to describe molecules.
“It is now possible to predict the properties of some complicated materials purely through computation without referring to experiment,” says Garnet Chan, Bren Professor of Chemistry, director of the Rudolph A. Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry at Caltech, and senior author of the study. “These first materials that we have studied are like a baby step, or a prototype problem, along the way to more complex phenomena such as high-temperature superconductors and quantum magnets.”
Garnet Chan, Bren Professor of Chemistry at Caltech. Credit: Caltech
The work, led by Linqing Peng, PhD ’25, and Tianyu Zhu of Yale University, was published in
. Both lead authors began working on the project in Chan’s laboratory at Caltech.
A simple effect exposes a hard problem
What makes the Kondo effect such a useful test is that the phenomenon is relatively simple to describe but much harder to predict quantitatively.
Place a single magnetic atom, such as iron or manganese, inside a metal such as copper and then cool the material. In an ordinary metal, electrical resistance steadily drops as the temperature falls, allowing current to flow more easily. With a magnetic impurity present, however, the trend eventually reverses. At a threshold known as the Kondo temperature, resistance reaches a minimum and then begins to rise.
“That is the signature of the Kondo effect, and it’s a property of the electrons in the impurity interacting with the electrons traveling through the bulk metal,” Chan explains.
Electron interactions reverse the resistance trend
The reversal is a visible consequence of a much more complicated interaction among electrons. The magnetic impurity contains unpaired electrons whose spin gives the atom its magnetism. At higher temperatures, the direction of this magnetic moment fluctuates freely.
As the metal cools, its electrons begin interacting more strongly with the impurity’s spin. They can flip their own spins in ways that partially cancel the magnetic moment of the embedded atom. Those interactions create additional scattering, producing the characteristic leveling off and eventual increase in electrical resistance.
At still lower temperatures, electrons throughout the surrounding metal collectively arrange themselves into a cloud that screens, or effectively cancels, the impurity’s magnetism.
Linqing Peng. Credit: Caltech
This collective behavior makes the Kondo effect a classic many-body problem. In such systems, the behavior of many interacting particles cannot be understood simply by examining each particle independently. Physicists established the broad theory of the Kondo effect in the 1970s, with important contributions from Caltech alumnus Kenneth Wilson, PhD ’61.
The same challenge appears in more complicated strongly correlated materials. In familiar materials used in computing, including semiconductors such as silicon, interactions among electrons are weak enough that they often have little effect on overall behavior. In strongly correlated materials, the motion of one electron can depend sensitively on what many other electrons are doing.
That makes accurate calculations especially important for researchers trying to understand quantum materials such as high-temperature superconductors and quantum magnets.
Real materials push beyond simplified models
The Kondo effect became a benchmark for those efforts because researchers can state the underlying problem relatively simply and already understand its broad physics. What they have struggled to calculate is exactly how the resistance changes or precisely where the Kondo temperature falls for a particular impurity inside a particular real material.
Traditional computational approaches make the problem manageable by stripping away much of that real-material complexity. They typically reduce the electronic structure to a small number of orbitals, regions around an atom’s nucleus where electrons are most likely to be found, and then apply an approximate mathematical model.
Tianyu Zhu. Credit: Caltech
Chan and his colleagues instead used computational tools from quantum chemistry to retain much more of the impurity’s actual electronic structure. Treating the magnetic atoms more like molecules allowed the researchers to calculate their interactions inside copper without relying on the same degree of simplification.
The seven transition-metal impurities provided a direct test of whether that more chemically faithful description could reproduce material-specific Kondo behavior. For most of the elements, it did so with substantially greater accuracy than the simplified model-based calculations.
A prototype for harder quantum materials
The systems tested so far are still far less complicated than the quantum materials researchers ultimately want to predict. But the results suggest that calculations incorporating the full chemical complexity of real materials are becoming practical for at least some strongly correlated systems.
“We are in an exciting era in which faithful predictive quantum descriptions of the full chemical complexity of real materials are coming within reach,” says Peng. “It is becoming realistic to predict material-specific behavior of correlated electrons from first principles, even in some of the most challenging classes of quantum materials.
“This is an important step toward computationally designing materials whose functions emerge from intricate correlated physics, such as high-temperature superconductivity, where the large chemical space and competition among many phases call for predictive theory to help focus the experimental search for new materials,” she adds. “I am excited to see what new materials breakthroughs this theory will enable in the future.”
Reference: “Toward an exact quantum many-body treatment of Kondo correlation in magnetic impurities” by Tianyu Zhu, Linqing Peng, Huanchen Zhai, Zhi-Hao Cui, Runze Chi and Garnet Kin-Lic Chan, 30 July 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.adq7402

title: NASA’s New Space Telescope Could Bring Alien Worlds Into View Like Never Before
content:
NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will test powerful new technology that could make faint exoplanets far easier to image directly. Credit: NASA
Now in space and undergoing commissioning, NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will test powerful new technology for directly studying exoplanets.
A planet orbiting close to a distant star can be extraordinarily difficult to see because the star’s glare overwhelms the much fainter light reflected by the planet. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will test a new approach designed to separate that faint planetary light from the much brighter star beside it.
The telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument, or CGI, will combine advanced coronagraphy with active wavefront control, using deformable mirrors to correct tiny optical imperfections and suppress stray starlight. If the technology performs as intended, astronomers could directly image and study gas giants that are older, cooler, and orbit closer to their stars than the hot, young planets typically found through direct imaging.
“The CGI aboard the Roman Space Telescope is the most technically sophisticated device for optical observations ever operated in space for scientific research,” says Oliver Krause, head of the Infrared Space Astronomy Research Group at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg.
Photograph of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope taken on 7 August 2026 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US. In preparation for launch aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket on 30 August 2026, it was carefully integrated with its payload adapter inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility. This specialized mount provides stability within the rocket and is designed for large, heavy loads. Credit: NASA/Jolearra Tshiteya
Roman launched from Kennedy Space Center
aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket on August 30, 2026, following roughly a decade of construction. The telescope was designed for a five-year primary mission with a possible five-year extension, but NASA now says fuel savings from its highly accurate launch and early trajectory correction could support at least
22 years of potential science operations
. Roman will investigate the history of the universe and the roles of dark matter and dark energy in cosmic expansion and the formation of large-scale structure.
Roman is currently traveling toward its final orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1 million miles (1.5 million kilometers) from Earth, where it is expected to arrive in early December.
Since launch, engineers have successfully powered on CGI and completed an initial checkout of its software, cameras, mechanisms, thermal controls, and other systems. The instrument is now undergoing months of calibration and testing before full science operations begin, when it will demonstrate technologies designed to make direct imaging of
exoplanets
far more powerful.
Roman is expected to
discover many new exoplanets
, while CGI will focus on a particularly difficult challenge: separating the faint light of planets from the overwhelming glare of their host stars. Its technology could expand direct imaging to worlds that are currently extremely difficult to observe.
Two techniques tackle stellar glare
A coronagraph uses specialized masks to block a bright star so that much fainter objects nearby can become visible. But those masks can produce strong image artifacts around the star. As a result, astronomers using this method have mainly detected Jupiter-like gas giants orbiting relatively far from their host stars, where they are easier to separate from the glare.
Fully populated optical bench of the CGI following delivery to NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. At its maximum dimension, the optical bench measures 1.7 meters × 1.7 meters. Credit: NASA/Chris Gunn (CC BY-NC-ND 2.0)
CGI adds active wavefront control to reduce these unwanted effects and improve the contrast between a star and a nearby planet. Two deformable mirrors, each controlled by more than 1,600 tiny actuators, can subtly change shape to compensate for minute imperfections and changes in the telescope’s optics. Similar deformable-mirror technology is used in adaptive optics on ground-based telescopes, but Roman will apply it with extraordinarily precise wavefront sensing and control in space.
Inside CGI, masks, deformable mirrors, and sensors will work together to suppress interfering starlight. The system is designed to detect a planet next to a host star that is a billion times brighter, roughly the contrast between Jupiter and the Sun. That would represent up to a thousandfold improvement over current capabilities.
An integrated spectrograph will then allow researchers to analyze the atmospheric composition of these planets. CGI is also intended to image circumstellar disks, the structures of material surrounding nearby stars, in visible light.
Extreme stability keeps CGI aligned
Achieving this level of performance requires extraordinary mechanical stability. Under Krause’s leadership, engineers and scientists at MPIA designed, developed, manufactured, and tested key components called Precision Alignment Mechanisms, or PAMs. These mechanisms precisely position optical elements such as filters, coronagraphs, and mirrors.
Over eight hours of operation, the PAMs must not tilt by more than 40 milliarcseconds. For comparison, 3.6 million milliarcseconds make up one degree. The required stability is equivalent to the apparent size of a person standing in Los Angeles when viewed from Heidelberg.
One of six flight models of the Precision Alignment Mechanisms (PAMs) for the Coronagraph Instrument (CGI), a camera aboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. The PAMs position and stabilize the optical elements of the CGI during observations. Credit: O. Krause / MPIA
MPIA, NASA’s sole direct German partner on CGI, is also helping develop software to process technical and scientific data and prepare observations. NASA’s Community Participation Program coordinates the measurements, with Krause serving as the local project lead and Wolfgang Brandner responsible for observations aimed at detecting gas giants in visible light.
During Roman’s ongoing commissioning, members of the program are evaluating data as the observatory’s instruments undergo calibration and testing. “However, thanks to the CPP’s global distribution, with members in the US, Japan, and Europe, our data analysts can carry out their tasks during normal office hours,” says Wolfgang Brandner.
Once routine operations begin, the data will be made publicly available immediately after processing at the Roman Science Support Center. NASA expects Roman’s first science images to be released in early 2027.
A path toward imaging another Earth
If CGI succeeds, its technology could be refined for future space observatories such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory. That could bring astronomers closer to directly imaging an Earth-like planet around another star.

title: NASA’s Chandra Reveals Galaxies Being Torn Apart, Blasted by Black Holes, and Reborn in Stars
content:
A barred spiral galaxy featuring a prominent central bar or bridge of stars that channels gas toward its core. Chandra X-rays (purple) highlight growing black holes along the bar and core, merged with Hubble optical light (white, yellow, and soft blue) and JWST infrared dust filaments (red). Studying barred spirals in action can help reveal how gas in our own Milky Way, which is also a barred spiral, feeds its central black hole and forms new stars. Credit: NASA/CXC/SAO; NASA/ESA/STScI/Hubble Heritage Team; NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI/J. Lee and T. Williams; NASA/CXC/SAO/L. Frattare, J. Major, K. Arcand
Galaxies can be peaceful star factories or cosmic wrecking grounds, torn apart by collisions and blasted by colossal black hole jets.
A new collection of 16 images from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory captures galaxies in radically different stages of their lives. The gallery combines decades of Chandra observations with data from NASA’s James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes, IXPE (Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer), Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array), and other observatories on Earth and in space.
Astronomers broadly classify galaxies as spiral, elliptical, or irregular. Spirals such as the Milky Way have arms extending from their centers, while ellipticals generally contain older stars and often bear the imprint of past mergers. Irregular galaxies have no single defining structure and can reflect collisions, intense star formation, or other disruptive events.
Why Astronomers Observe X-Rays
Visible light shows stars and dust, but X-rays reveal some of the most violent activity inside galaxies. Chandra can detect gas heated to millions of degrees, compact stellar remnants, debris from exploded stars, and material energized by growing supermassive black holes.
These phenomena help shape galaxies and spread chemical elements into space. Exploding stars and powerful outflows distribute material that can eventually become part of new stars, planets, atmospheres, and living organisms.
This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. Credit: NASA/CXC/SAO
Combining X-rays with infrared, optical, and other observations allows astronomers to examine the same galaxy in several complementary ways. Each wavelength highlights different structures, producing a more complete picture of how galaxies form, interact, and change over cosmic time.
Studying distant galaxies also gives astronomers valuable context for understanding the Milky Way. Because researchers cannot observe our galaxy from the outside, neighboring systems provide useful comparisons and possible clues to its past and future.
Spiral Galaxies Seen From Different Angles
Face-on galaxies such as Messier 33 and NGC 3938 give astronomers a largely unobstructed view of their spiral arms. These structures contain energetic stellar pairs, regions of active star formation, and the remains of powerful cosmic explosions.
NGC 1672 and NGC 1385 belong to a different class known as barred spirals. Their elongated central structures contain stars, gas, and dust that can channel material toward the inner galaxy, supplying the raw ingredients for new bursts of star formation.
NGC 4725 shows another way that stars can begin forming. Evidence suggests that an earlier encounter with another galaxy disturbed its material and helped trigger new stellar growth.
Edge-on views reveal features that are harder to see when looking directly at a galaxy’s face. NGC 4631 (the Whale Galaxy) and Messier 82 (the Cigar Galaxy) display enormous halos and superwinds of million-degree gas. Repeated stellar explosions have driven this material thousands of light-years into intergalactic space, carrying newly produced elements with it.
Black Holes That Reshape Galaxies
A supermassive black hole can become an active galactic nucleus when it consumes surrounding material. Although the black hole itself emits no light, the matter falling toward it can become intensely hot and release radiation, outbursts, and narrow jets powerful enough to affect the wider galaxy.
In Centaurus A, Chandra and IXPE reveal a jet of high-energy particles extending tens of thousands of light-years from the galactic center. The observations help researchers examine how particles are accelerated near one of the most extreme environments in the universe.
A large spiral galaxy that is being stripped of its gas as it plunges at high speed through hot gas in the Virgo Cluster of galaxies. Chandra’s X-ray data (magenta) pinpoints high-energy point sources—such as X-ray binaries and supernova remnants—and diffuse hot gas nestled within the spiral disk imaged by Hubble (blue, brown, and gold). A ground-based optical light image taken from New Mexico by Timothy Martin reveals red filaments of hydrogen gas streaming over 300,000 light-years behind the galaxy as it falls into the Virgo Cluster. Credit: NASA/CXC/SAO; NASA/ESA/D. Thilker/J. Lee/PHANGS-HST Team; Tim Martin; NASA/CXC/SAO/L. Frattare
The central black hole in Messier 106 produces jets that heat nearby gas and create unusual spiral structures. Unlike ordinary spiral arms dominated by stars, these features are shaped largely by energy released from the galaxy’s active core.
The Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104) contains a supermassive black hole within an immense central bulge of stars. Around its prominent dust lanes, Chandra maps a diffuse halo of million-degree gas and a population of hot stellar remnants.
Collisions, Rings, and Stripped Galaxies
Several images capture galaxies undergoing dramatic gravitational upheaval. In Arp 143, a direct collision generated an expanding ring resembling a cosmic bullseye and sent waves of star formation through the system.
NGC 3256 and the dust-shrouded starburst II Zw 096 are caught in violent mergers. Such collisions were more common in the early universe, when galaxies were closer together, and they can compress gas, accelerate star formation, and transform the structures of the galaxies involved.
These mergers also provide a rough preview of the Milky Way’s distant future encounter with Andromeda. Although individual stars are unlikely to collide because of the enormous distances between them, gravity will profoundly rearrange both galaxies.
NGC 1569 serves as a nearby laboratory for investigating the powerful starbursts that helped shape young galaxies. NGC 660 has an unusual “polar ring,” with stars and gas orbiting over the galaxy’s poles, likely preserving evidence of a past gravitational interaction.
Messier 90 is experiencing a different kind of transformation as it travels through the Virgo Cluster. Pressure from the surrounding environment is violently removing its star-forming gas, gradually depriving the galaxy of the material needed to produce future generations of stars.

title: Scientists Discover an Unexpected Connection Between Stem Cells and Childhood Brain Tumors
content:
Researchers found that certain brain tumor mutations may keep developing cells trapped in a stem-like state. Credit: Shutterstock
A blood stem cell molecule revealed how some childhood brain tumor mutations disrupt CoREST and led researchers to existing drugs worth testing further.
A molecule used to help blood stem cells multiply has led researchers to an unexpected connection with childhood brain cancer. Scientists at
Lund University
found that the molecule produces a cellular effect similar to one caused by genetic mutations in a subgroup of aggressive brain tumors in children.
The connection could help researchers understand how these tumors develop and has also pointed them toward existing drugs that may be worth investigating as future treatments.
The molecule, called UM171, was developed by researchers at Université de Montréal. In stem cell research, it is used to increase the number of blood stem cells outside the body while helping them remain stem cells rather than mature into blood cells. Producing more of these cells can provide enough for transplantation in people with serious blood diseases.
Blood stem cell research reveals a cancer link
Previous research, including work at Lund University, showed that UM171 acts through a protein called KBTBD4. This causes an important group of proteins in the cell, known as CoREST, to break down.
That mechanism caught the researchers’ attention because genetic mutations involving KBTBD4 can produce a similar effect in some childhood brain tumors.
Agatheeswaran Subramaniam, research group leader at Lund University, Sweden. Credit: Åsa Hansdotter, Lund University
“The same structure in the cell is also affected by mutations in the KBTBD4 gene, genetic changes that occur in a subgroup of aggressive brain tumors in children. Although the causes differ, the result is the same — the structure breaks down,” says Agatheeswaran Subramaniam, researcher at Lund University.
Some of these tumors are medulloblastomas, the most common malignant brain tumor in children. About 15 to 20 children in Sweden develop medulloblastoma each year.
Medulloblastoma belongs to a group called embryonal brain tumors. These cancers are thought to develop when immature cells in the growing brain fail to mature normally and instead continue dividing. Tumors associated with KBTBD4 mutations are particularly difficult to recreate in the laboratory because they arise early in brain development.
Cancer mutations keep cells stem-like
Although UM171 and the cancer-associated mutations both disrupt CoREST, there is an important difference. The molecule’s effect is temporary, while the mutations can cause a lasting shortage of CoREST and leave cells in a stem cell-like state.
“It is striking that a small molecule and genetic mutations lead to the same effect in the cell. But while the molecule has a temporary effect, the mutations instead lead to a long-term shortage of CoREST, meaning that the cells remain in a stem cell-like state. This may contribute to the development of embryonal tumors,” says Rohit Sivaprasad, doctoral student at Lund University.
Existing drugs counter the mutations in lab tests
That similarity gave researchers a way to investigate whether drugs might counteract the effects of the KBTBD4 mutations. In a large-scale drug screen, they identified a group of drugs called HDAC inhibitors that did so.
HDAC inhibitors affect gene activity inside cells. Because drugs in this class are already approved for other uses, the researchers describe the approach as drug repurposing, which means investigating an existing drug for a different disease.
The finding points to a possible path toward future treatment, but it remains at an early stage. The experiments were conducted in the laboratory using blood stem cells, not medulloblastoma tumors, so researchers still need to determine whether the drugs work against the tumors themselves.
“What is fascinating about research is that sometimes you find a fundamental mechanism that can help answer several different clinical questions. This study was carried out in the laboratory using blood stem cells. The next step is to test whether these drugs work in medulloblastoma tumors,” concludes Agatheeswaran Subramaniam.
Reference: “Cancer-associated KBTBD4 mutations induce differentiation defects and confer a unique therapeutic vulnerability” by Rohit Sivaprasad, Kristijonas Žemaitis, David Linfeldt, Sudip Ghosh, Anne de Snaijer, Mattias Magnusson, Fredrik Ek, Jenny Hansson and Agatheeswaran Subramaniam, 10 August 2026,

title: Yanhe's flexible perovskite solar module begins in-orbit testing aboard a Chinese satellite
content:
Yanhe's flexible perovskite solar module begins in-orbit testing aboard a Chinese satellite
Yanhe Technology
(formerly Yanhe Solar), the Chinese flexible perovskite PV developer, has launched its self-developed flexible perovskite module into orbit aboard the Tianyi-52 satellite, which lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on September 17. The company says this is China's first module-level, full-operating-conditions in-orbit engineering validation of flexible perovskite PV technology in the commercial space sector.
The module now begins long-term performance monitoring in orbit, where it will be evaluated under high vacuum, temperature cycling between -100°C and +100°C, high-energy particle irradiation, and atomic oxygen erosion. Yanhe will track electrical output, interconnection reliability, and mechanical stability, with data relayed in real time through the satellite's telemetry system.
The launch follows through on plans Yanhe
outlined earlier this year
, when it said its tandem perovskite modules had passed simulated extreme space environment tests and that multiple satellites carrying its solar cells would launch in 2026, en route to a goal of over 100 satellites by 2028. It also comes a month after the company
finalized the engineering prototype
of its "Nebula" flexible roll-up space solar wing.
Yanhe said it plans further in-orbit validation later this year covering other technology pathways, including flexible silicon cells, perovskite-HJT and perovskite-CIGS tandem cells, module arrays, and complete solar array wings.

title: Long-lived 'hot' electrons in tin perovskites could push solar cells past 33% efficiency
content:
Long-lived 'hot' electrons in tin perovskites could push solar cells past 33% efficiency
Researchers at the University of Groningen and TU Wien have identified the physical mechanism behind the unusually long "hot carrier" cooling times previously measured in tin-based perovskites, a property considered essential for a next-generation solar cell architecture aimed at exceeding the standard efficiency ceiling for single-junction devices.
Band filling and the hot phonon bottleneck combine to stretch carrier cooling times in tin perovskites into the nanosecond range. Credit: Faber et al., ACS Energy Letters
A hot-carrier solar cell (HCSC) works by extracting photo-excited charge carriers before they shed their surplus energy as heat, potentially pushing efficiency past the Shockley-Queisser limit of about 33% that caps conventional single-junction cells. The approach depends on carriers staying "hot" for nanoseconds rather than the picosecond timescales typical of most semiconductors. Several recent experimental studies on tin-based metal halide perovskites reported cooling times reaching several nanoseconds, but the physics driving this behavior had remained unclear.
Using ensemble Monte Carlo simulations benchmarked against previously published time-resolved photoluminescence measurements of CsSnI
, the team showed that the ultra-long cooling times arise only when two effects act together: the dynamic Burstein-Moss effect, in which low-energy states fill up with excited carriers and block further relaxation, and the hot phonon bottleneck, in which carriers reabsorb heat-carrying phonons faster than the phonons can decay away. Neither effect alone was sufficient to reproduce the measured cooling times.
In the simulations, cooling stretched from about 4 picoseconds with both effects switched off to about 470 picoseconds with both active at a carrier density of 3×10¹⁸ cm⁻³, in line with an experimentally measured value of about 636 picoseconds. The team also found that carriers affected by this mechanism remain "hot" in terms of their Fermi-Dirac temperature, not just their average kinetic energy, staying above 600 K even 200 picoseconds after excitation at the highest carrier densities tested - a distinction that matters because it is this thermodynamic temperature, rather than raw carrier energy, that determines the voltage boost an HCSC could theoretically deliver.
Based on these findings, the team proposed three material design criteria for future hot-carrier absorbers: a low effective mass to maximize the Burstein-Moss shift, which points toward tin-based compositions over their lead-based counterparts; a soft phononic lattice with low-frequency optical modes to lower the threshold for the phonon bottleneck to form; and high material purity, since defects tend to open additional pathways that accelerate rather than extend carrier cooling.
"The measurements were clear, but we didn't understand the physics behind this," said Jan Anton Koster, professor of Physics of Novel Semiconductors and Devices at the University of Groningen and the study's corresponding author, noting the team "even started to doubt the measurements ourselves." Adding the hot phonon bottleneck to the simulations "slowed the loss of energy, but not enough to explain our measurements," Koster said. Only once band filling was included as well did the simulated energy loss stretch into the nanosecond range, matching the experiments carried out by co-author Maria Antonietta Loi, professor of Photophysics and Optoelectronics at the university.

title: 国新办就“促进能源绿色转型与供应保障”举行中外记者见面会-索比光伏网
content:
为充分展现能源行业奋进新征程、建功新时代的伟大实践和能源领域一线奋斗者扎根基层、开拓创新的感人事迹，国务院新闻办公室9月23日（星期三）下午在北京市（华电）集中式光伏项目暨荒滩治理示范基地举行“新征程上的奋斗者”中外记者见面会。国家能源局组织中国石油、国家电网、中国华能、中国华电、国家能源集团5位能源领域基层一线代表，围绕“促进能源供应保障与绿色转型”主题与中外记者见面交流，5位代表各自分享了在二氧化碳捕集利用与封存、配网不停电作业、海上光伏风电平台研制、“沙戈荒”光伏+生态治沙、煤矿智能化开采等领域内攻坚克难、自主创新的亲身经历和动人故事。见面会后，在北京市集中式光伏项目暨荒滩治理示范基地及密云水电厂进行实地采访，了解光伏、水电发展情况。
国务院新闻办新闻局 王师:
各位记者朋友，下午好！很高兴在秋分时节和大家一起参加在户外举办的国务院新闻办“新征程上的奋斗者”中外记者见面会。
能源是国民经济的命脉，关系着国计民生和千家万户，是不可忽视的“国之大者”。保障能源安全、推进绿色低碳转型、建设能源强国，离不开千千万万扎根一线的能源领域的工作者们。
今天，我们很高兴邀请到五位能源领域代表，请他们围绕“促进能源供应保障与绿色转型”这一主题和大家交流。他们是：国家电网北京电力昌平供电公司技术总师、配网不停电作业室班长王月鹏先生，中国石油吉林油田二氧化碳开发公司技术带头人张德平先生，中国华电甘肃腾格里绿色能源有限公司党委委员、副总经理郑三国先生，中国华能清洁能源技术研究院海上风电部主任、智慧水电部主任刘鑫先生，国家能源集团神东煤炭锦界煤矿综采一队党支部书记、队长赵云飞先生。
下面请五位代表介绍一下他们自己，首先有请王月鹏先生。
国家电网北京昌平供电公司技术总师、配网不停电作业室班长 王月鹏:
各位中外记者，大家好！我是王月鹏，来自国网北京昌平供电公司，任技术总师，也是配网不停电作业室的一名班长。
大家知道，配电网是连通千家万户的“电力毛细血管”，我从事的专业就是在配电网万伏高压上带着电进行工作，也被誉为万伏高压线上的“手术师”，我们用专业保障老百姓可靠供电。入行26年以来，我一直扎根带电作业一线。对于普通人来说，万伏高压是禁区，但是对于我们来说，那是保障首都可靠供电的阵地。
我参加工作后，一直都在努力创新。今天，我给大家带来了一个小物件，它叫双C型线夹安装工具。我们在给线路安装线夹的时候，就好比在给线路做缝合手术，但是我们所面对的“病人”却有些特殊，因为它自带万伏高压，危险系数非常高。我们在操作的时候就要远离它，而这个工具的成功研发就可以让我们作业人员远离万伏高压完成工作，可以说安全和效率是“双提升”。与此同时，它也填补了国内技术空白。
装备在不断迭代升级，我们的作业手段也在不断丰富。从最初的人工作业，到现在使用我们自主研发的国内首套含引流线预处理功能的带电作业机器人，变的是装备，不变的是“人民电业为人民”的初心。
用上电、用好电、不停电就是最好的服务，我们多流一滴汗，老百姓家中就多亮一盏灯。我会继续扎根带电作业一线，和团队一起把技术练得更精、把服务做得更好，用心守护好首都的万家灯火。谢谢！
下面有请张德平先生作介绍。
中国石油吉林油田二氧化碳开发公司技术带头人 张德平:
各位媒体记者朋友，大家好！我叫张德平，来自中国石油吉林油田二氧化碳开发公司，主要从事二氧化碳捕集、利用、封存的科研生产工作。
我手里拿的这张照片，就是我们CCUS国家示范工程的现场实景。简单来讲，CCUS就是将二氧化碳捕集起来，封存到地下，并且把油“挤”出来，实现变废为宝。
国家从战略层面高度关注能源低碳转型和二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存，在重大科技专项中作出了重要的攻关部署。在国家能源局的统筹指导下，中国石油积极实践低碳战略，设立了一系列科研攻关任务，我非常荣幸参与到这些攻关任务当中。项目刚开始的时候，国内没有成熟的技术，也没有现成的装备，也缺少现场实践经验，一切都得从零开始进行摸索。我们的团队扎根井场，日夜驻守攻关，一遍一遍试验、复盘和优化，慢慢摸索出陆相油藏二氧化碳驱油与埋存的规律，逐步探索形成了特色技术系列，其中多项填补了国内行业的技术空白。
据我了解，我国石油行业现在已累计注入二氧化碳近2000万吨，其中吉林油田已经超过了400万吨。我们还获得了国家授权专利、参与编制了国家和行业的技术标准近百项，埋存规模走在了国内前列，让老油田焕发了绿色新生。
作为新时代能源战线的奋斗者，接下来我将继续坚守科研一线，扎根现场，继续攻关，用实干守护好国家能源安全。谢谢！
下面有请郑三国先生作介绍。
中国华电甘肃腾格里绿色能源有限公司党委委员、副总经理 郑三国:
各位记者朋友，大家好！我叫郑三国，来自中国华电甘肃腾格里沙漠河西新能源基地。
2011年参加工作以来，我一直扎根新能源建设一线，我现在所在的甘肃腾格里沙漠河西新能源基地，是国家“沙戈荒”大型风电光伏基地重点项目之一，项目位于腾格里沙漠腹地武威市九墩滩。刚到九墩滩的时候，那儿的植被覆盖率还不足5%，我和我的同事们在前人治沙成果的基础上，探索了“生态+生产+民生”的治理模式。四年下来，147万株耐旱植物在那儿扎下了根，植被覆盖率提升到70%以上，治沙面积达到1.8万亩，同时还提供了800多个就业岗位。我们探索实践的这套治沙模式同我国其他“沙戈荒”项目基地一样，为促进我国可再生能源发展和生态环境治理提供了有益探索，同时也取得了重要成效。
我手里的这张图，生动地展示了我们项目治沙前后明显的对比。经过我们的努力，这儿的生态系统优化很快，目前我们正在全力推进甘肃省单体容量最大的光伏治沙项目建设，等项目建成以后，我们的治沙面积还将新增6万余亩，年增发绿电50多亿度，节省标准煤158万吨，减排二氧化碳434万吨。
我出生在河西走廊，从小就在风沙里长大，现在我能够亲身参与家乡的蜕变，看到家门口的黄沙一点点披上“绿装”，老乡们在家门口就能有稳定的收入，我心里非常高兴。这些成绩的取得，不是我一个人的，是我们所有驻守在戈壁滩上的同事们一点点努力奋斗来的。
欢迎大家到我们九墩滩光伏治沙基地去看看，看看我们在荒漠“种”出来的绿色。谢谢大家！
下面请刘鑫先生作介绍。
中国华能清洁能源技术研究院海上风电部主任、智慧水电部主任 刘鑫:
各位记者朋友，大家好，我叫刘鑫，来自华能清洁能源技术研究院，是一名海上新能源科研工作者。简单地说，我的工作就是在大海上“追风逐光”，把海上的风和阳光变成清洁的电，送到祖国各地。大家看我手上这套“黄海一号”模型，把这个模型的面积放大约6万倍就是它的实际大小，相当于4个篮球场那么大，大家形象地叫它“六边形战士”，如今这位“战士”正在山东半岛海域上，搭载着434块不同技术规格的光伏板以及2台垂直轴风机，开展着一系列海上试验。作为我国已经建成的水深最深、抗浪能力最强的海上漂浮式光伏平台，它可以抵抗约10米巨浪。大家肯定很好奇它的本领是怎么炼成的呢？我们把它设计为9米高，海浪够不着上层甲板，光伏组件就不会被海水侵蚀。大家也很容易想象到，平台高了就会变厚重，为了破解这个难题，我们团队从零开始搭建专用的仿真模型，首创了钢塑混合轻量化浮体，大家可以理解为相当于给这个平台套上了一个很轻便的“游泳圈”，平台的重量也随之减轻。向海而行，“风光”无限。未来我将不断探索创新，我相信，稳稳的绿色电能，就是大家稳稳的绿色幸福。谢谢！
下面有请赵云飞先生作介绍。
国家能源集团神东煤炭锦界煤矿综采一队党支部书记、队长 赵云飞:
主持人好，各位记者朋友大家好，我叫赵云飞，来自国家能源集团神东煤炭锦界煤矿，现任综采一队党支部书记、队长，是一名一线矿工。
以前，大家说起煤炭行业觉得它技术不够先进，如果用四个字概括就是“苦、脏、累、险”。但是现在随着智能化的快速推进，煤炭行业也正在变成一个实实在在的高技术行业。在我们矿井已经投用了55类133种矿用机器人，智能化确确实实降低了工人的劳动强度，改变了作业条件，生产工效也实现大幅提升。
我2018年开始接触煤矿智能化技术，刚接触的时候，我觉得智能化技术就像一盏明灯，让我看到了煤炭行业的发展前景，也看到了煤矿工人崭新的未来。但是在这个项目刚推进的时候确实遇到了非常多困难，因为在工作面安装了大量智能化设备，程序运行不稳定，故障频发，后期维护任务也特别多；我们的工人操作的时候，操作方式也发生明显变化，所以当时挑战非常大。但是我坚信智能化这条路一定能够走通，也一定要走通，我就带头研究学习新技术，在现场每一项新技术投入到工作面使用的时候，我都会到现场盯着这个技术反复试验，确保设备能够安全稳定之后再投入运行。目前，在我们矿区，智能开采、绿色开采、超长工作面开采等一批新技术新工艺正在落地应用。
今年，我们公司新招聘了1500多名大学生，其中研究生比例占到了15%，越来越多高学历人才走进煤矿，实现了技术创新与人才队伍的双向赋能。我坚信，未来的煤矿肯定会向着安全、高效、绿色、智能的方向持续迈进。谢谢大家！
谢谢五位代表！接下来进入提问环节，提问前请通报所在新闻机构。
中国能源传媒集团中国电力报记者:
我的问题想提给郑三国先生。我们了解到，您在推进“沙戈荒”大基地建设的过程中，创新提出了“生态+生产+民生”的融合治理理念，也实现了我们荒漠治理和绿电开发的同步推进。我想请问这套治理理念在我们项目现场是如何落地实施的？为当地的生态改善和群众增收具体带来了哪些变化？谢谢！
谢谢您的提问，我想很多人一听“沙戈荒”，第一反应应该就是四个字：大风、黄沙。当时我们去现场的时候，那真是“风吹沙跑、遍地荒凉”，别说种树，连棵草都难扎下根。但偏偏就是这片不毛之地，变成了我们新能源发展的绿色宝地。我们当时就琢磨，能不能在这儿既能把绿电发出来，还能把沙治住，这就是您刚才提出的“生态+生产+民生”的融合治理模式。说通俗一点，就是把治沙、发电，还有富民三件事捆在一起干，让同一片地既能长绿、还能发电、还能富民。
在工程的实施过程中，我们主要靠三招。
第一招就是工程固沙。我们项目使用螺旋桩，把螺旋桩像拧螺丝一样钉在沙里，尽量减少对地表的扰动，同时配套草方格施工和锁边工程，这样就可以把流动的沙丘牢牢“钉”在原地。
第二招就是生物固沙。我们坚持以水定绿、因地制宜的原则，选种梭梭树、花棒等耐旱植物，让这些植物在沙地里面扎下根、连成片，就像筑起了一道“绿色长城”。
第三招就是科技赋能。我们连同高校一起攻关，从植物的养育到选型，形成了一整套的“近自然”修复技术，我们拿下了18项国家专利。现在，我们的这套打法已经成为全国“沙戈荒”生态治理的示范样板。
说到实实在在的变化，我现在每到现场去的时候都深有感触。生态上，我们累计种植梭梭、花棒等植物147万株，撒播草籽3.6万斤，治理荒漠1.8万亩。同时，我们这一片的地表固沙率也达到85%以上。以前这儿黄沙漫天，现在在那，我们的黄羊、野兔、沙狐都已经成群结队地在我们场站里安了家，这就说明我们的生态系统真正地恢复过来了。
至于民生上的变化，我们也是看得见、摸得着的。项目带动我们周边群众就近务工，也给他们带来了稳定的就业岗位，让他们从传统的体力劳动者变成了拥有一技之长的技能型人才。说到底，我们干的这件事，就是把不毛之地真正的“点沙成金”，让黄沙变绿地、绿地生绿电、绿电富百姓，把群众增收、绿电开发协同推进，一起受益。
总台中国之声记者:
今天的各位代表都是在能源一线扎根多年，亲历了我国能源产业从传统向绿色智能转型的跨越，可以说在各自领域都攻克了关键的技术难题，有的甚至实现了全球领先。回顾从“跟跑”到“领跑”的历程，在攻坚克难的过程中，支撑各位一路坚守、不断突破的力量是什么？另外，我们也想了解一下，哪个瞬间让各位觉得这份职业十分有价值？谢谢！
我先来回答这个问题。我觉得支撑我一路走下来的力量，简单概括为一个词就是“责任”。我在清华大学的专业是能源动力，我觉得，我有责任运用我所学的知识，推动我国新能源技术的自主创新，让海上风电技术有能力走向更远的“深蓝”，也有责任让千家万户用上更加清洁高效的绿电，就是“为你能，尽我能”。
我再跟大家分享一下我觉得很有价值的一个瞬间，就是我们研发的垂直轴风机，在南极的中山站和秦岭站发出华能第一度绿电的那一天。这个绿电来得非常不容易，因为大家都知道，南极极寒、大风，普通的小风机在南极根本扛不住，叶片说吹断就吹断。为了能让我们的风机扛住这份考验，我们研究出了专属的翼型和冰雪地基，让它能够在冰天雪地中立得牢、转得动。还记得当时调试发电的那一天，因为是通过卫星通讯联系的，到了预定的时间之后一直没有消息，我心里很忐忑。直到整个风机顺利投运的消息传来后，整个团队非常激动，因为我们研制的技术在南极真正派上了用场。那一刻，我们一路走过来的艰辛都变成了满满的自豪。
我就分享这些。谢谢！
下面我跟大家作一些分享。整个项目从最开始攻关的时候，我就参与其中。参加工作20多年，我一直在科研一线和大家一起攻克二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存这项技术。回顾这个项目从最初“跟跑”到“领跑”的过程，一路走来非常不容易。项目推进过程中遇到很多问题，很多技术方案都经历了上百次推倒重来。其中有一个典型问题，是二氧化碳强腐蚀问题。因为二氧化碳对管线和设备会造成很大的破坏，我们在攻关当中屡屡受挫，经过多次反复试验、反复调整，最终才形成低成本的二氧化碳防腐技术。
支撑我们长期坚守扎根一线的，一方面是“双碳”战略赋予我们的时代使命，另一方面是我们能源人的初心。我们一直致力于将这些核心技术牢牢掌握在自己手里，把这些关键技术难题给它啃下来。
要说戳中我内心的那一瞬间，是我们自主研发的一些技术走出国门、亮相阿斯塔纳世博会、世界石油天然气大会，那一刻我们广大同仁付出多年的辛苦、持续攻关，终于得到了大家的认可，内心的成就感是难以言说的。谢谢！
我也分享一下我的故事。说实话，我当时第一次到九墩滩的时候，内心也是非常发怵的，在那儿白天晒得人头发晕，入秋之后冻得人发抖，当时有人就问我们，你们在这儿图个啥？我说我们图的是信念，图的是把这儿的荒滩变成绿洲，让这满地的“黄沙”变成让乡亲们增收的“金沙”。说白了，我们干的这件事，就是把那些“生态负资产”一点点地变成“绿色正资产”，把“不毛之地”变成“希望之地”。
九墩滩的风沙“脾气”很大，一场风过来，半条路都能被埋了。现在不一样了，我们的光伏板一片片加起来了，草方格一块块支起来了，风沙到这儿就慢了，沙子也被牢牢地“钉”在了原地。今年春天下了几场雨，我去现场巡视的时候，发现金色的草方格之间已经冒出了点点绿芽，正是这片绿色，让我更加坚信我们“板上发电、板下治沙”这条路走对了。光伏治沙的路还很长，九墩滩的光伏板还在一片片地往前铺，治沙的草还在一茬茬地往上长。但是我们始终相信，只要我们信念不移、干劲不减、初心不改，一茬接着一茬干，一棒接着一棒跑，我们始终坚守的绿色目标终有一天能够实现。谢谢！
广东广播电视台粤TV记者:
我想请问张德平先生，您前面介绍的碳捕集、利用与封存技术，是全球公认的助力碳中和的关键技术，从实验室到大规模的工程应用，大家很关心技术落地的现实挑战。请您结合自身一线技术，谈一谈这项技术在国内的实践成效，项目成功的背后有哪些攻坚克难的故事？在未来，还能够从哪些方向持续突破？谢谢！
谢谢您的提问。我们最开始实验的时候，国内没有可以参考的成功案例，所有的工作都得从零开始去摸索。中国石油集团将二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存国家示范工程落地在吉林油田，但是实现的路还需要我们去一点一点蹚出来。
印象最深刻的就是二氧化碳冻堵。实验室里模拟的数据看着都非常好，但是一到现场，一接到管道和设备上就会出现这样那样的问题，因为二氧化碳和水接触会产生水合物，从外观看就像是冰和雪一样的固体，它会堵塞井筒、管线和阀门，造成注入压力增高，甚至注不进。特别是在东北冬天的晚上，气温零下二三十摄氏度，一旦接到现场的电话，不管多冷，我们都往现场赶。我们经常裹着厚厚的棉袄在寒风中守设备、在井场调参数，经过一遍一遍试验、复盘和优化，才逐步摸索出适用于现场实际的处理方法。
在中国石油的整体规划和部署下，吉林油田二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存示范工程，逐步从我们最初的构想落地为现实。现场建成了全国首个全产业链二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存示范基地。一路走来，我们不但把二氧化碳注到地下，实现了驱油增产，还建成了适合我们自己的特色技术系列，把低碳发展和能源保供衔接了起来。
要说CCUS技术未来的发展，还要从以下三个方面持续突破。第一是在成本管控方面，全套二氧化碳从捕集、输送到注入，花钱比较多，我们还需要在低成本的材料、国产化的装备上持续发力，把成本降下来。第二是在源-储匹配方面，因为我们有大量的排放源，如何把碳源和埋存地高效衔接起来，还需要在现场进行示范和探索。第三是在系统耦合方面，二氧化碳捕集、利用与封存技术如何与风、光新能源进一步搭配耦合，进一步发挥我们的价值，还需要在现场多跑、多试。
技术不能只停留在展厅和论文里，要想实现真正落地，就得我们一批人持续扎根现场，把一个一个难题给它解决掉，才能真正更好发挥我们CCUS减碳保供的作用。谢谢！
我的问题想提给王月鹏班长。您刚才提到，带电作业机器人的落地应用大幅降低了一线作业人员的安全风险，提升了配网供电的可靠性。在研发落地推广的过程中，您还遇到了哪些难题？目前机器人作业还有哪些待优化的方向？下一步您团队的攻关重点是什么？谢谢！
感谢您的提问。带电作业机器人在研发过程中，确实遇到了很多困难。
我们遇到的困难，第一就是作业场景。世上没有相同的鸡蛋，带电作业也没有相同的现场。它不同于标准化流水线的机器人，作业环境的光线是非常复杂的，另外作业的杆型也是多种多样，还有导线也比较多，可能会重叠。所有的这些叠加在一起，再加上风的作用，进行动态识别和定位就非常困难。我给大家举一个简单的例子，人要是去取一样东西，眼到手到，非常简单，但是机器人靠的是算法识别定位。在这过程中，即使导线出现很小的偏移，它都要持续进行识别定位后才能抓取。我们在攻关过程中，遇到了很多类似这样想着很简单、但却需要投入大量精力去解决的问题，我们都一个个攻破了。
第二个就是作业时间，换一个说法就是作业效率。虽然有了带电作业机器人以后，不需要人直接参与作业，但依然需要人去配合作业。每一项的作业时间也是作业人员特别关注的参数之一，如果说效率上不去，一线人员不爱用，就没办法推广。再给大家举一个小例子，就是我们在作业的时候，发现机器人做每一项工作都需要来回更换不同的末端工具，效率很低。能不能解决这个问题？我们就研发了三合一的末端工具，可以把导线举升、绝缘层剥除和导线连接三合为一，效率就大大提升了。
最后一个就是专业认可。装备做出来了，最主要的是得让一线人员觉得好用、能用、愿意用。我们的目标就是操作简单、好上手，即使工作经验和理论经验不深的一线员工，依然一学就会、一看就懂。我们做出来的样机，第一时间就先放到一线模拟使用，让他们一遍一遍地帮我们把关，最终得到他们的认可。
今后我们的发展方向，重点要攻破的就是带电作业机器人和绝缘斗臂车的协同控制问题，因为现在机器人和斗臂车是两个独立的主体。机器人要到达作业位置，需要作业人员手动操作绝缘斗臂车送到作业点。以后，我想让带电作业机器人作为大脑控制绝缘斗臂车，到达任何一个它想到的作业点，这样的话就相当于给机器人踩了一个“高跷”，让它更智能。谢谢！
总台央广网记者:
我的问题提给赵云飞队长，您刚刚也介绍了煤矿智能化的持续迭代升级，不少人关心的是矿工这个职业未来会走向何方？站在一线队长的角度，您认为技术革新会为煤矿工人带来哪些变化？谢谢！
感谢您的提问。首先我作为一名扎根一线多年的矿工队长，确实经历了煤矿从传统的“拼人数”到智能化的完全转型，随着技术的发展，我觉得煤矿对当代煤矿工人的职业认同、职业价值，还有职业取向发生了很明显的变化。以前我们谈论煤矿工人的时候，总觉得是靠力气、靠流汗，但是现在随着5G、AI还有智能化的普及，我们的采煤设备已经实现了远程的操控和自主协同。并且我们的煤矿工人已经从原来的“操作者”变成了坐在监控室里的“监控者”和“数据分析师”，这种变化不仅体现在我们的工作强度还有安全风险降低了，更体现在职业价值转变为对智能复杂系统的驾驭，还有对设备隐患的精确诊断。我们的矿工不再是单纯的普通矿工，更像是保障国家能源安全的“技术工匠”或“智慧矿工”。
另外我想说的一点是，技术进步给我们煤矿工人带来了更多的职业尊重感，我们在现场通过“师带徒”或者常态化的技能培训，鼓励更多的老矿工学习新技术，同时鼓励新入企的员工到现场去井下学习实操。通过不断学习，不仅能保证他们有稳定的收入，而且可以自信分享自己的技术经验。在我看来，职业成就感体现明显。另外，我们煤矿提倡“自保、互保、联保”，在智能防控的加持下，安全红线意识也深入人心，对生命负责、对企业负责、对社会负责的态度，也正是新时代产业工人责任和担当的体现。
总之，我觉得智能化不是淘汰矿工，而是成就矿工，让矿工的职业价值更加凸显，让他的职业定位更加坚定。未来，我相信煤矿一定会通过技术和知识推动传统的采矿业迈向更安全、更高效的新阶段。谢谢！
我的问题提给郑三国总经理和刘鑫主任的。在“双碳”目标下，“沙戈荒”新能源大基地和深远海海上风电光伏都是能源绿色低碳转型的核心赛道。请问这些技术成果分别为能源绿色低碳转型带来了怎样的价值？在下一步规模化推广中，还有哪些需要突破的关键点？谢谢！
谢谢您的提问，关于“沙戈荒”的核心价值，我想总结为三句话：
第一，它是我国绿电增量的“主力军”，也是我国绿电的“大粮仓”。当前，我国已有3批基地接茬投运，拿我们九墩滩300万千瓦项目来说，项目建成以后，每年有50亿度的绿电通过“陇电入浙”特高压通道送到浙江。
第二，它实现了能源开发和生态治理的“双赢”。光伏板架起来以后，板下蒸发量减少约15%—30%，地表输沙量减少约50%以上。以前人们觉得沙漠是“生态包袱”，现在它正一点点变成“绿色资产”——板上发电、板下长草，一分地干了两份活儿。
第三，它带动了西部欠发达地区的产业升级和民生改善。绿电不光能“送得出”，还能“用得上”。中卫数据中心绿电直供项目，每年产生绿电22.9亿千瓦时，直接驱动算力产业发展。同时，在就业上提供了3500多个就业岗位，让老乡们在家门口就能有稳定的收入。
关于规模化推广。我个人认为主要还有两方面需要突破：第一，统筹做好新能源开发与外送通道建设时序问题，同时提升新能源就地消纳转化水平，协同推进“源网荷储”和绿电直连，让电既能“送得出”，还能“用得上”。第二，提高对高寒、高海拔、强风沙、弱电网的极端环境适应性，这不仅是对工程建设的挑战，也对技术创新提出了新的要求。要把技术创新落到复杂的项目施工现场，把大基地作为天然“实验室”，把不利的自然条件转变成有利的实验资源。
郑总讲了“沙戈荒”，那我来谈谈深远海海上风电和光伏。它的核心价值用一句话来概括就是，把我们辽阔的大海变成绿电的“粮仓”。我国东部沿海省份用电量很大，但土地金贵，而深远海风光资源充沛，离东部用电负荷中心又近，电可以就近发、就近用，并且不占用陆地，也不占用农田。我们的“黄海一号”已经用实测的数据证明了，深远海光伏可以“发得出”、也可以“稳得住”；再通过“风光同场”开发，让同一片海域可以产出更多的绿电，服务于“双碳”目标的实现。
关于下一步规模化推广，我认为要解决“三个关键”：第一是成本。我们通过浮体轻量化、设计标准化，还有产业链协同，要持续把造价降下来，让老百姓能够用得起深远海的绿电。第二是可靠性。深远海的风浪、盐雾腐蚀环境，比近海要苛刻得多，我们的设备要能够承受得住长年在深远海“独自站岗”，设备运行维护也要更加智能化、无人化。第三是统筹规划。无论是海域利用、生态保护，还是并网送出等，我们需要协同推进，并和海水制氢等新业态相结合，让一片海能有多份收获。谢谢！
每日经济新闻记者:
筑牢国家能源安全底线，离不开一代又一代能源人的坚守付出。如今，传统能源行业也在朝着智能化、数字化、绿色化快速转型，老一辈技术经验和新一代数字化技术如何融合互补，来保障民生用电和能源供应安全稳定？另外，结合自身从业经历，代表们对想要进入能源领域的年轻人，有哪些职业建议和寄语？新时代能源行业需要青年具备哪些核心能力？谢谢！
我先跟大家结合自己的亲身经历分享一下，我是1998年技校毕业，上班的第一课，我的师父彭新立就给我树立了一个特别优秀的榜样，他是国网北京市电力公司配网带电作业第一代领军人，那辈人在条件极其有限的情况下，把带电作业从零做起、做大做强。他们的经验非常丰富，也非常宝贵。刚才跟大家分享了我牵头研发的带电作业机器人，所有的基础数据、经验数据都是依靠师傅们积累下来的，再进行不断更新迭代，让带电作业更加安全，让百姓用电更加可靠。三伏天的时候，家里面空调吹出的徐徐凉风；三九天的时候，家里面的阵阵暖意；夜晚灯火通明……所有的这些都有带电作业人在背后默默付出与坚守。
结合这些，我想和准备或者是希望来到我们专业的年轻人说，一定要沉着冷静、胆大心细、敢于创新、敢于探索、敢于突破，只有这样，才能把老一辈的匠心和新一代的数字技术相结合，推动专业和行业发展。
我也有很多徒弟。我的感触就是对于徒弟的培养因人而异，他们有自己的特点，有的人喜欢创新，有的人喜欢动手，有的人善于总结，不能用一个模子把他们全部雕刻出来，要让他们发挥自己的能力，目的是什么呢？能够培养他们的兴趣，有了兴趣，他才会热爱这个专业，热爱这个专业才能更深扎根，才能走得更远。谢谢！
我结合自己的工作经历也谈一下我的感受。我觉得我们老一辈技术工人的技术经验就像“压舱石”，新一代数字技术更像是“推进器”，只有把两者融合互补起来，才能更好发挥作用。举个例子，比如说我们以前的老工人，他们靠声音、震动就可以判断设备故障、设备隐患，但是我们的智能化系统又能实时监测设备的温度、压力这些数据，我想只有把我们老工人的这些经验的诊断方法转化为数据分析模型，才能让我们的智能化系统预测更精准，这样就实现了“人防+技防”，这就是“经验+数据”的力量。
另外，对进入煤炭行业的年轻人，我给他们的建议，第一就是要有“跨界融合”的能力，首先既要懂采矿的原理，又要懂数据运维。结合我自己的经历，我原来是学采矿的，但是干了七年机电，这些工作经历对我后来搞智能化帮助很大。因为智能化它是两个学科的一个融合。第二个，我觉得他们既要有创新思维，又要有吃苦耐劳的精神，因为守护万家灯火毕竟不是一句口号，需要我们踏踏实实、实实际际干下去。谢谢！
我的问题提给刘鑫主任。我们注意到，除了“黄海一号”，您的团队还在攻关全球最大的直驱型深远海漂浮式海上风电机组。请问未来把风电和光伏建在同一片海上，互补发电的开发路线是什么样的？您心目中未来我国的“海上电站”又是什么样的？谢谢！
谢谢您的提问。首先我想说，我国海域辽阔，风光资源充沛，怎么能够更高效、更安全地用好这座能源宝藏，是我们的探索方向。未来的开发路线和发展趋势，我总结起来有三句话：从近海走向深远海，从固定式走向漂浮式，从单一发电走向风光互补融合开发。
首先，从近海走向深远海。这是我们开发海洋能源的空间主线。我们坚持“近海打基础、深远海探新路”：一方面，在海南、江苏等地开展固定式海上光伏研究，积累近海大规模开发建设和运行经验；另一方面，依托“黄海一号”在深远海真实海况中逐点采集数据，实打实去验证深远海开发的可行性，为后续规模化开发蹚出新路。
第二，从固定式走向漂浮式。这是我们挺进深远海的技术趋势。我们联合研制的17兆瓦直驱型风机，是目前全球单机容量最大的直驱型漂浮式风电机组，单台年发电量约6800万度，可以满足约2万户家庭一年的用电需求，还可以抵御17级台风，目前这个风机已经顺利下线。从“固定扎根”到“漂浮逐浪”，技术的创新和升级让我们真正具备了开发深远海风电资源的底气。
第三，从单一发电走向风光互补融合开发。这是我们的长远追求。海上的风和光具有天然的错峰特性，同场运行可以让电力输出更加平稳，同时还可以共享一片海域，共用一条送出线路，这样可以大幅提升资源的利用效率。
至于你说的未来我心目中“海上电站”是什么样子，我想，它应该是一座“蓝色能源岛”，海上的风和光“同台合唱”，白天“追光”，夜里“捕风”，并和海水制氢、海洋牧场、海上算力等各种新业态深度融合，组成一个多功能集成的“海上枢纽”，让绿电海上来、点亮千万家。这就是我们科研人的梦想，也是我们正在建设的未来。谢谢！
我想问赵云飞一个问题，关于煤炭的。今年中国煤炭产量不太多，最近价格越来越贵。你觉得煤炭产量可以很快恢复吗？
感谢您的提问。上周，我所在的国家能源集团针对煤炭保供进行了专门部署。作为一名一线区队长，我会认真落实上级部门的生产任务安排，发挥好智能化采煤优势，科学组织生产，合理安排设备检修，全力以赴保证煤炭稳产稳供。同时，作为一名区队长，我肯定会带领区队员工坚守现场，用实干履行岗位职责，把保供任务分解到现场的每一道工序中，为国家能源稳定供应贡献基层力量。谢谢！
谢谢几位代表的分享。从他们的分享中，我相信大家都能感受到能源事业的发展凝聚着许许多多能源工作者的心血。让我们持续关注能源发展，倡导绿色低碳生产生活方式，共同守护能源安全，共享美好宜居生活。

title: 生态环境部：退役光伏组件按工业固体废物强化监管-索比光伏网
content:
9月22日，生态环境部举行9月例行新闻发布会。生态环境部固体废物与化学品司司长钟斌出席发布会，介绍固体废物和新污染物治理工作情况。生态环境部新闻发言人裴晓菲主持发布会，通报近期生态环境保护重点工作进展，并共同回答记者提问。
钟斌表示，近年来，退役光伏组件、风电设备、动力电池等“新三样”固体废物受到广泛关注，其回收利用和污染防治成为新能源产业健康发展必须解决的问题。举个例子：可能不少人没见过非法处理废弃光伏板，我们同事讲：光伏组件通常采用层压/封装工艺，拆解分离难度较大，为了把材料分离开，一些小作坊采取简易焚烧方式，现场弥漫着刺鼻的气味。
生态环境部联合有关部门持续完善相关环境监管体系，主要开展了以下三方面工作。
首先，完善法规政策。针对退役光伏组件、风电设备主要是发电企业产生的特点，生态环境法典明确退役设备处理责任，从事风电、光伏发电建设运营的企业应当自行或者委托具备条件的企业对退役风电机组叶片、光伏组件等进行循环利用或者无害化处置;针对退役动力电池主要是社会源产生的特点，明确了动力电池生产者责任延伸制度，要求生产者按照国家规定，以自建或者委托等方式建立与产品销售量相匹配的废旧产品回收体系，履行回收和利用责任。国家发展改革委、工业和信息化部、生态环境部、商务部、国家能源局等部门密切配合，制定出台了退役光伏组件、风电设备、动力电池回收利用的相关政策，初步建立起全生命周期闭环管理体系。
针对处理中的污染问题，生态环境部牵头制定污染防治相关标准。先后发布废锂离子动力蓄电池处理、废光伏设备回收处理污染控制技术规范，正在制定废风电设备回收处理污染控制技术规范。重点对退役动力电池黑粉焙烧和金属回收、废光伏设备层压件分离、废风电叶片无害化处置等环节提出污染防治要求。
针对非法处理情况，加大监管执法力度。前面提到，我们在全国开展非法倾倒处置固体废物专项整治行动，其中将非法拆解处置退役新能源设备、退役动力电池等列为重点，要求严厉打击非法拆解处理等环境违法行为，倒逼退役设备流向正规利用处置渠道。工业和信息化部也部署开展规范废旧动力电池回收利用联合执法专项行动。如，广东省东莞市整治废动力电池拆解乱象，集中查封一批非法拆解窝点。
下一步，生态环境部将立足职责，积极推动“新三样”固体废物循环利用和污染防治，重点是针对不再用于发电用途的退役光伏组件、风电设备，按照工业固体废物强化监管。针对退役动力电池，配合有关部门落实生产者责任延伸制度，推动更多退役动力电池进入正规回收渠道。加强回收利用企业常态化执法监管，打击污染严重的非法拆解处置退役设备行为。
