title: Envision Energy launches next generation offshore wind turbine
content:
Envision Energy has announced its next generation EN-252/16.7 offshore
wind turbine. The turbine is designed to deliver higher energy production,
increased reliability and improved project returns.
The turbine has a rated capacity of 16.7 MW and features a high performance
rotor tailored specifically for the European market. The design incorporates
vertically integrated component technologies, advanced safety and grid
capabilities, and AI powered lifecycle monitoring.
The swept area to power ratio is approximately 2.99 square meters per kilowatt.
For GW offshore wind farms, the turbine can deliver around 1% to 2% higher
annual energy production.
Christian Schrimpf, executive vice president of offshore wind at Envision
Energy, said: "The next phase of offshore wind is not simply about
increasing turbine scale. The real value of scale lies in how effectively
it translates into higher energy production, greater reliability and stronger
economics across the project lifecycle."
The design is based on Envision Energy's proven Model Z platform, which
has more than a decade of offshore operational experience.
Extensive testing has been carried out, including drivetrain system loading
tests and more than 600 hours of accelerated life testing to assess drivetrain
system interactions under challenging operating conditions.

service operation vessels supporting the offshore wind sector.
Purus and Siemens Gamesa will continue their existing relationship through
the new long-term agreement.

offshore wind farm
in Germany.

and Guarantees of Origin (GoOs) and provide balancing services.
Nordergründe has an installed capacity of 110.7 MW, enough to power around
90,000 households annually. The wind farm comprises 18 turbines located
around 13 kilometres off the coast of Lower Saxony in the German North
The company said Nordergründe was the first German offshore wind project
where all major components were supplied and installed by local manufacturers.
“Skyborn has recently taken full ownership of Nordergründe, the project
has been generating renewable electricity for almost a decade,” said Christian
Zaum, Chief Financial Officer, Skyborn Renewables.
For InCommodities, the agreement marks its entry into offshore wind, adding
it to a renewable asset management platform that continues to expand.

title: Van Oord reveals two next generation flexible fall pipe vessels
content:
Van Oord reveals two next generation flexible fall pipe vessels TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Van Oord reveals two next generation flexible fall pipe vessels
Van Oord has unveiled Vindnes and Vestnes, two next-generation flexible
fall pipe vessels.
The vessels are expected to strengthen Van Oord's subsea rock installation
capabilities while supporting offshore wind, interconnector and other critical
infrastructure projects.
Designed from the keel up as dedicated subsea rock installation vessels,
the vessels will enhance safety, operational efficiency, installation performance
and future fuel flexibility, according to Van Oord.
The design aims to maximise productivity while minimising environmental
impact. To achieve this, the vessels balance carrying capacity, installation
rates, fuel efficiency and offshore workability.
Maurits den Broeder, managing director of Offshore Energy at Van Oord,
said: "We are investing not only in additional capacity, but in a
new generation of purpose-built subsea rock installation vessels designed
around productivity, efficiency and sustainability."
He added: "These vessels reflect our confidence in the continued growth
of offshore energy and reinforce Van Oord's commitment to remaining at
the forefront of seabed intervention."
The flexible fall pipe vessels are currently under construction at Yantai
CIMC Raffles Offshore in China, with delivery expected in 2028 and 2029.

title: Pacifico Energy secure survey license for Nam Trung Bo 3
content:
Pacifico Energy has secured sea survey licence approval for the development
of the 1.3GW Nam Trung Bo 3 offshore wind project.
The approval was granted by Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment
and allows Pacifico Energy to carry out technical and environmental studies
to evaluate the approved offshore area.
Preliminary desktop assessments of the site and a detailed survey campaign
will be undertaken in preparation for field activities.
The field programme will include geotechnical and geophysical surveys,
wind measurement, meteorological and oceanographic studies, environmental
baseline surveys, and other technical investigations.
The project, located in Lam Dong Province, was identified in Vietnam's
Adjusted Power Development Plan VIII and is expected to begin commercial
operations between 2031 and 2035.
"It reflects our long-term confidence in Vietnam's offshore wind potential
and our commitment to supporting the country's energy security and sustainable
growth," said Nate Franklin, founder and group chairman of Pacifico
Pacifico Energy emphasised its commitment to supporting Vietnam's growing
electricity demand, with offshore wind expected to play a crucial role
in the country's energy transition.

title: Are GPU Loans Safe From Rising Rates?
content: The Federal Reserve’s recent rate hike, and rising expectations of another soon, put a fresh spotlight on financing arrangements for the wide array of companies borrowing money to pay for AI data centers and chips. Rates are rising just as investors have been growing more skeptical about AI-related debt in general, a potentially potent mix for higher borrowing costs for new deals across the board. But in one corner of the AI financing market that might sound the worst off—floating-rate loans used by major GPU buyers—some of the biggest loans have already been engineered to blunt the impact of higher benchmark rates, for now at least. CoreWeave has borrowed billions in recent years to pay for Nvidia’s graphics processing units via delayed draw term loans, a structure others including Iren and Nscale have begun to embrace too. Many of these deals have hedges built in that are meant to effectively turn much of their floating-rate exposure into fixed rates. These DDTLs, which are generally drawn down as the GPUs are purchased and deployed, are often initially structured with floating interest rates for at least some of the borrowing capacity. For instance CoreWeave’s largest DDTL, an $8.5 billion facility, is roughly split between floating rate and fixed-rate portions. That means that the interest rate on some of the financing can change frequently, unlike that on a fixed-coupon bond, commonly used in AI data center financing. The interest rate on the floating portion of many DDTLs is based on short-term gauges like the secured overnight financing rate, which typically moves with changes in the Fed’s benchmark rate, plus a fixed spread on top. SOFR was 3.87% as of Sept. 23, up from a recent low of around 3.5% in May, though it remains below its year-ago level. Some GPU financings use a version called Term SOFR, a forward-looking rate that’s around 4% right now on a three-month basis. Meanwhile, recent big GPU loans have carried spreads ranging from roughly 2.25 percentage points to 5.5 percentage points added to SOFR-based benchmarks. Spreads can vary widely based on factors like the creditworthiness of the customer ultimately using the GPUs. But for the floating-rate component, some of the biggest GPU borrowings also have significant hedges against rising rates. Those are generally derivatives such as interest rate swaps, where a borrower pays a counterparty a fixed rate while receiving a floating rate. For example, CoreWeave was hedging at least 75% of anticipated floating-rate borrowing under a $2.6 billion GPU facility from last year, filings show. The floating portion of the company’s newer $8.5 billion facility, meanwhile, will be subject to a hedging requirement of at least 95% of anticipated borrowing. And Nscale’s $1.85 billion GPU facility for a data center in Ward County, Texas, requires interest-rate hedges covering between 90% and 110% of its projected floating-rate borrowing, according to credit agreements the company disclosed as part of its recent initial public offering filing. Nscale’s other large U.S. GPU facility, a $1.2 billion loan for a North Carolina project, has a similar hedge requirement. There are arguably some benefits of the DDTL structure itself. Interest on DDTLs generally starts accruing only once the money is drawn, though borrowers may pay a smaller, separate fee on the undrawn commitment. So a buyer of GPUs can secure a big pool of money but only pay interest as it draws the funds to buy and deploy the hardware. But all that doesn’t mean borrowers can ignore rate risk entirely, especially when it comes to contemplating new borrowing. Hedge requirements have already been written into some loan agreements, which limits how much exposure companies can leave floating. But for new facilities, companies or their lenders may still have to decide how much exposure to leave unhedged. Of course, AI infrastructure providers can look to tap a wide range of financings beyond DDTLs, and in general companies shift between sources of financing based on investor appetite and market pricing. There’s a buffet of options for finding cash that includes vendor financing and private credit as well as bonds and convertible debt, plus issuing equity. But those aren’t all necessarily well suited to financing GPUs specifically, since borrowers spend money on the GPUs over time. And CoreWeave, for its part, has told investors that its DDTLs are structured so debt payments line up with contractual payments from its own customers. Spreads have widened on investment-grade AI credit lately, and new issuance has been coming in pricier than the broader market, while some lower-rated AI data center project debt has seen investors demand especially high yields . Convertible debt can keep interest costs down but come with potential dilution for shareholders. In other words, finding attractive financing may be getting tougher regardless. And part of why AI borrowing is getting more expensive isn’t related to rates—at least not directly. Investors have been swamped with new supply while questions about the ultimate payoff of AI investments remain largely unanswered. Overheard: Who Buys All the AI Debt? Jas Khaira, head of Blackstone’s AI-focused investment team, said on Wednesday that there are still some big questions about what kind of investors will step up to continue financing the AI industry’s infrastructure buildout. “We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt,” he said at The Information’s AI Agenda event in San Francisco, responding to an audience question about whether financing costs will have to rise in order to fund the buildout. “We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from.” He noted debt markets for investment-grade companies and the private credit market as potential sources of capital. He said that while public markets are large, debt will “probably clear at a higher price because of the quantity getting pushed.” And how exactly big companies like OpenAI and Anthropic will finance their compute needs remains uncertain. “A lot of that is going to depend on their ability to go public,” he said, “and their ability to be investment grade over time.” New From Our Reporters Exclusive Wall Street’s GPU Futures Push Stalls at the CFTC By Dakin Campbell Exclusive Luckey’s Erebor Bank Plots Syria Expansion By Michael Roddan Jane Street-Linked Data Center Debt Sours By Dakin Campbell Q&A Bridgewater’s Jensen Wants AI Compute Giants Regulated Like Big Banks By Dakin Campbell

title: What I Learned From AI Agenda Live
content: What a day! I loved meeting many of our amazing subscribers yesterday at our AI Agenda Live conference, where my colleagues and I interviewed leaders from companies like OpenAI , Google DeepMind , Nvidia , Blackstone , Replit , Atlassian and more. Discussions at the conference touched on topics ranging from whether Google can catch up in the AI race to how companies are managing the runaway costs of AI to who is going to buy the debt being raised to fund the data center buildout. (For a full recap, check out this story from my colleagues here .) Here are three themes I’m thinking about from my conversations at the conference. 1. The price wars and open-source AI. Replit CEO Amjad Masad told me onstage that his company is likely using less open-source AI these days than at the beginning of the year because of how aggressively the labs—and OpenAI in particular—have cut the costs of their models. That’s great for developers who are looking to manage their AI costs, especially as agents use more tokens than ever. However, what this means for the AI labs themselves is less clear. I asked Alexander Embiricos , OpenAI’s head of enterprise product, why the company has been so aggressive with cutting the costs of its models rather than holding onto some of those savings to boost its gross margins. Embiricos said that the company wants to slash the price of its models to encourage adoption because many users just aren’t using as much AI today as they could be because it’s unaffordable. That might be admirable, but I’m not sure that public market investors will be as enthused with that argument when they’re looking at OpenAI’s margins in its IPO filing. 2. Alternative model architectures are back. Jev , a new model that started to blow up this week for its impressive speed and low costs, came up during at least three different panels on Wednesday. Jev uses a different architecture from the large language models underlying popular products like ChatGPT and Claude ; rather than outputting paragraphs of text written in full sentences, it produces outputs of numerical responses and probability estimates, which indicate how confident the model is in its response. Though Jev isn’t quite as accurate as leading large language models, as Atlassian chief product and AI officer Tamar Yehoshua said on Wednesday, it’s much cheaper and faster. Plus, because it provides a confidence score for its responses, users can make more informed decisions on when they decide to rely on Jev’s responses or not depending on how confident the model is. All of this means that Atlassian can not only find tasks where they can replace LLMs with Jev, but also tasks where they weren’t able to use an LLM in the first place due to cost or speed concerns, said Yehoshua. 3. The capability overhang is very real. One idea that leaders at OpenAI and other AI labs have spoken about is the “capability overhang,” or the idea that there’s a big gap between users’ dim awareness of what AI can do and what AI can actually do. Part of Embiricos’ job consists of trying to close that gap by building new features that exploit models’ underutilized capabilities and show users what models can actually do. “Even if models stopped progressing today, there is a bunch more product work that we can do,” he said. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Meta Platforms announced partnerships with Walmart and other retailers for its AI agent Muse days after e-commerce giant Amazon blocked the personalized agent from accessing its shopping site. An AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked an Australian government website in June, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said on Wednesday. The AI accessed both public and nonpublic data from the country’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service website, Albanese told reporters, adding that the country is now investigating whether other government systems were breached. Anthropic said that Claude helped discover a previously unknown enzyme system that the company said could represent a new gene editing tool akin to CRISPR , which has transformed the creation of new gene therapies. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei briefed the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday as part of the international organization’s General Assembly week in New York. In a session on artificial intelligence and international security, the two executives addressed concerns around the technology while defending its potential to cure diseases and solve complex math problems. People on the Move OpenAI has hired Patreon co-founder Sam Yam to lead a new creator product division, Creator Product , Yam announced Wednesday on X, a sign of renewed interest in attracting consumers. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. DeepSeek is aiming to complete its second funding round by the end of October as it prepares to go public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, The Information reported on Thursday. The company’s fundraising efforts may be fuelled by a boost in revenue, which has hit $1 billion on an annualized basis. It is targeting to raise 50 billion yuan ($7.5 billion) at a valuation of 500 billion yuan ($74.5 billion). Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in cloud and AI infrastructure across Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE between now and 2030, plus a further $400 million in subsea and terrestrial data connectivity for the region. Modal Labs and Baseten , two startups that help companies run AI models in production, are separately in talks to raise new funding at sharply higher valuations, Bloomberg reported. Modal is in talks at a roughly $15 billion valuation—about triple the $4.65 billion mark it hit in a round four months ago—while Baseten is in talks at a $26 billion valuation, more than double the $13 billion valuation it reached in June. Tekever , a Portuguese-British maker of AI-powered surveillance drones, raised $580 million in the first close of a Series D funding round led by UC Investments and Baillie Gifford , at a $6.4 billion valuation. Bessemer Venture Partners announced on Wednesday that it has raised $5.75 billion across two new funds to invest in AI. Enveda , a Colorado biotech that uses AI to discover medicines, raised $311 million in a Series E funding round at a $2 billion valuation led by Catalio Capital Management . Brahma AI , whose AI helps create audio and video content for media, sports, healthcare and advertising companies, raised $150 million of a $250 million round through the issuance of preferred shares, including $100 million from Multiples Alternate Asset Management . Basecamp Research , a London biotech that designs medicines with AI trained on genetic data from more than 30 countries, raised $140 million in an oversubscribed Series C funding round led by S32 . Numeral , whose AI handles sales tax compliance for businesses, raised $100 million in a Series C funding round led by Insight Partners . Ema , whose AI “employees” handle HR, IT and finance work for large companies, raised $77 million in a Series B funding round led by Creaegis . UltraSight , whose AI guides non-specialists through cardiac ultrasound scans, raised $24 million in a Series B2 funding round led by Alive HealthTech Growth Fund . C.H.BECK , a major German legal publisher, became the majority shareholder of Noxtua , a Berlin legal-AI company, through a Series C funding round of more than €100 million that also brought in Austria's MANZ as a new investor. Flock Safety , whose AI-powered cameras read license plates for police departments and businesses, is weighing a potential sale and has held preliminary talks with outside advisers, Semafor reported. Meta announced a host of upcoming updates for its AI assistant product Muse , including that it will soon be available in Meta smart glasses, that it will be able to run on users’ Mac and that it will get its own email address. The company also announced a Tamagotchi-like wearable for the assistant. Amazon is giving the merchants that sell goods on Amazon’s site 12 free months of Quick Plus , an AWS AI workplace assistant, Amazon announced Wednesday at its annual conference for sellers, Amazon Accelerate. Quick Plus normally costs users $20 a month. Chinese AI researchers have increasingly opted to stay and work in their home country , leading China to become the top destination for elite AI talent, according to a study by think tank Carnegie China . Google released two new text-to-speech models, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS on Wednesday. YouTube is releasing a new AI storytelling assistant to help creators analyze scripts and rough cuts of their videos, the video-streaming company announced Wednesday. title: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic AI Safety Group Takes Shape
content: Google , OpenAI and Anthropic are pushing forward with a plan to create a new AI safety-focused standards body on their own, without government oversight, in hopes of launching it by the end of the year or early in 2027, according to people familiar with the matter. The three companies tentatively plan to name the self-regulatory organization the Standards Authority for Frontier AI, the people said. Some members of the working group have considered an array of well-known figures to be CEO. They approached Sriram Krishnan, a former venture capitalist and top AI policy adviser in the Trump administration, for the position, according to people familiar with the matter. The members also considered Arati Prabhakar, former director of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy during the Biden administration, for the CEO role. Meanwhile, Condoleezza Rice, former U.S. Secretary of State, and David Friedberg, an entrepreneur and venture capitalist who also hosts the “All-In” podcast, were on a shortlist for the role of the chair, who would advocate on the group’s behalf with the U.S. government, the people said. The companies also had a shortlist of possible scientific advisers for the organization, including Beth Barnes, the founder and CEO of METR, an AI research nonprofit, and Paul Christiano, an adviser to the Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation who was recently appointed to OpenAI’s foundation board. Some of the people on the shortlists said they had not been approached, and it’s unclear if the candidates are still under active consideration. The effort by the three AI giants aims to create a self-regulatory organization for companies building the most advanced or frontier models, at a moment when concerns about AI risks are at a fever pitch. Initially, the companies envisioned forming an industry-led group with oversight by the federal government, though that effort for a public-private partnership has stalled in the Trump administration. Still, as gridlock continues in Congress ahead of November’s midterm elections and the White House appears hesitant to advance new AI policy, SAFA would fill the vacuum through self-regulation. The standards body would perform key functions such as supporting third-party organizations that conduct testing of models before they’re deployed and laying out how AI developers should report safety and security incidents. The group would also define what the voluntary safety and security commitments the labs have previously made would look like in practice and establish qualifications for independent auditors of the models and labs, according to people working on the initiative. The working group members are also discussing whether SAFA itself should conduct safety and capability testing on models. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation is currently tasked with doing those tests, but some members of the working group are concerned that it doesn’t have enough resources to thoroughly test frontier models. Some members of the working group are advocating for SAFA to add other types of testing and evaluation on top of CAISI’s, said people familiar with the matter, although it remains unclear whether there would be overlap. The group is still debating the topic. The three companies have been holding discussions about the standards body for several months, The Information previously reported . The idea of a self-regulatory organization for AI entered the public discussion in July, when then–Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis published an essay laying out a proposal for such a body reporting to the government. He modeled it after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which oversees U.S. broker-dealers and securities professionals. For a time, there was interest in the proposal inside the White House, which went as far as drafting a potential executive order that would have established such a group. But progress on the order stalled amid opposition from other industry leaders including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to people familiar with the matter. Both have expressed public skepticism about advancing new AI regulation. The White House told Google, Anthropic and OpenAI that they had to find industry consensus on the standards effort before getting the government involved in it, according to people familiar with the matter. While the current plan is for SAFA to operate independently, some representatives of the companies involved are optimistic that it could have a relationship with the U.S. government in the future, the people said. Regulatory Vacuum Recent incidents involving advanced AI models have escalated calls for action on AI, including one in which a swarm of OpenAI agents hacked the open-source repository Hugging Face during a safety test. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google themselves have joined the chorus of government voices calling for, in essence, a timeout on the technology. Earlier this month, for example, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei advocated in an essay for the “pacing” of model development. The Trump administration, however, has publicly rebuffed any pleas for government intervention and slowing model development, instead arguing that the companies should proceed themselves on safety considerations. As the project continues without government oversight, it faces a number of other obstacles. Its mission appears to overlap with that of existing organizations such as CAISI and the White House’s voluntary framework for pre-deployment testing, as well as previous attempts to create industry safety groups. That includes the Frontier Model Forum, a nonprofit organization created in 2023 by Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft with many of the same goals as SAFA. One person who worked on Frontier Model Forum, which remains active, said companies and politicians often respond to perceived crises by creating a new organization, describing such efforts as “performative.” Still, a person familiar with the SAFA discussions said the goal is to have an industry-led organization that can operate more efficiently than the Frontier Model Forum. The two organizations could still work together and are in close contact, said people familiar with the conversations. A looming question for SAFA is whether the three labs can get wider industry support for the group. SAFA’s mission would be to provide supervision for labs building advanced models at the frontier, an often vaguely defined term for state-of-the-art models. That’s why Google, OpenAI and Anthropic—all of which are generally regarded as having the most advanced models—are developing plans for the group, according to people familiar with the initiative. That means other companies, including Meta Platforms and an array of companies building open-source models, would likely not currently fall under the organization’s evaluation remit. Those companies, however, would likely later qualify once their models cross the frontier threshold. SAFA would determine standards and benchmarks governing which models are subject to the group’s oversight, said one of the people, though it remains unclear how membership would work. That has led to skepticism from industry leaders outside the three companies, who have concerns that SAFA would create a regulatory bar boxing out the competition, including open-source model developers, according to critics of the plan. While Google, OpenAI and Anthropic continue discussions on launching SAFA behind closed doors, their executives have publicly advocated for the need for shared safety standards, especially as they push for further international coordination. It remains unclear which government bodies will lead the charge for these standards outside the industry. In a speech delivered to the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. “They must be shaped through democratic processes, by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” he said.

title: DeepSeek’s Annualized Revenue Hits $1 Billion as Startup Finalizes $7.5 Billion Fundraising
content: DeepSeek’s annualized revenue run rate has hit $1 billion, more than double the rate of a few months ago, buoyed by a recent price hike as well as continued popularity of its models, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The latest revenue figure, shared by CEO Liang Wenfeng in a recent meeting with investors, could boost investor confidence as the company finalizes its second funding round and as it prepares to go public in the Shanghai Stock Exchange. DeepSeek is aiming to complete the fundraising by the end of October, with a goal of raising 50 billion yuan ($7.5 billion) at a valuation of 500 billion yuan. DeepSeek’s revenue growth was driven in part by a price hike last month, which increased the costs of its models for customers by 2.3 to 4.5 times. Despite the price hike, DeepSeek’s models continue to cost among the lowest in major language models, and Liang said at the meeting that the price hike didn’t cause a decline in DeepSeek’s customer base, as user demand remains strong, according to the people. DeepSeek’s V4.1-Flash, released earlier this month, and the older V4-Flash, boast capabilities comparable to much larger models and have attracted customers around the world looking for AI systems that can power autonomous agents without breaking the bank. While DeepSeek’s revenue is still minuscule compared to U.S. AI model developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI , the company is achieving a healthy gross profit margin. The Information reported in July that DeepSeek’s annualized revenue run rate had reached between $400 million and $500 million, and the gross margin for selling access to its models through its application programming interface in the first seven months of this year was 82.9%, higher than both Anthropic and OpenAI during similar periods. That’s because DeepSeek has managed to keep the costs of running its models low, through methods such as improving the efficiency of its AI infrastructure so that the AI systems can perform tasks using fewer chips. Despite the growth, generating more revenue hasn’t been a priority for DeepSeek, Liang told investors in the meeting on Sunday, which imposed strict terms for participants to prevent leaks. The company generates revenue almost entirely by charging for access to its models through APIs. DeepSeek’s popular chatbot app, which is free to use with no advertising, generates no revenue. DeepSeek continues to put the majority of its resources into the development of new models. The company is allocating more than 70% of its computing capacity to model training, while reserving less than 30% of its compute for inference, or the running of existing models, Liang told investors during the meeting, according to the people. Liang also told investors that DeepSeek’s internal tests show its smaller models can run well on graphics chips designed for gaming, according to the people. He said such models can handle most of the everyday tasks users need. If DeepSeek can use gaming chips to run more of those tasks, it could ease the shortage of computing capacity available for inference without diverting too many of its most powerful chips from training. There is precedent for that: after the release of DeepSeek’s R1 model last year, demand and prices for Nvidia gaming chips on China’s black market surged. Over the past several months, Chinese AI models have rapidly increased their global presence, as the performance of their affordable open-source models narrows the gaps with that of U.S. frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Earlier this month, Z.ai, the Beijing-based developer of the GLM series of models, said its annualized run rate reached $1.8 billion. MiniMax, another Chinese competitor, said its annualized run rate jumped to $800 million in August from $150 million in February. Cheaper ways to run existing models may help DeepSeek serve more users, but developing new models still requires substantial compute capacity. For DeepSeek, one of the biggest challenges ahead is how to secure enough compute to train its new models amid U.S. export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced chips. Liang told investors during Sunday’s meeting that a major priority for his company is to use more domestic chips to train its models, adding he expects Huawei Technologies to start delivering training chips to DeepSeek as early as the fourth quarter this year, The Information reported earlier this week. Another concern for investors is Beijing’s investigation into potential data leaks to Anthropic. The Information reported on Tuesday that China’s internet regulator is investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot AI after Anthropic alleged both companies had been routing sensitive user data to Claude models.

title: Open Source, Model Price Cuts Keep AI Costs Under Control
content: Open-source models as well as cheaper model releases from Anthropic and OpenAI are helping business customers rein in costs while getting as much or more out of AI, said speakers at The Information’s AI Agenda Live conference in San Francisco Wednesday. “The existence of open source [models] adds pricing pressure on the labs, which is great,” said Amjad Masad, CEO of coding assistant Replit. Still, for many companies, it’s unclear how much value they’re getting out of AI spending. Only one in ten companies can show where return on investment is happening in its profit and loss statement, said Dan Diasio, global AI leader at consulting firm EY. “Most of the scaling has been based on enthusiasm as opposed to that evidence,” he said. The conference included speakers from Google DeepMind , OpenAI, Blackstone, Uber and cloud provider Nebius. Excerpts from the sessions are below. Uber Flattens Spending on AI Tokens Uber has managed to keep its spending on AI tokens largely flat in recent months despite wider internal use as it found ways to operate more efficiently, according to Mattie Toia, the company’s vice president of engineering and infrastructure. The ride-hailing company has been trying to make better use of AI and keep costs under control after earlier use of AI coding tools caused it to blow through its annual AI budget just a few months into this year. Toia said in the last three to four months measures including memory-optimization to avoid redundant computations and incorporating extensive Uber-specific data have helped keep AI costs stable. Uber’s use of more powerful open-source AI models helped bring costs down as well, Toia said. Enterprises are shifting from token-maxxing—where employees at companies used as much AI as possible to show they are embracing the technology—to what Nebius Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky called “value-maxxing.” “What you’re looking for is, how do I actually optimize the value that I’m creating for the cost?” Boroditsky said. Mattie Toia, Uber Boroditsky said Nebius is open to selling compute capacity based on achieving the outcomes business customers want, rather than charging based on Nvidia’s graphics processing units per hour. Nebius has experimented with spot-pricing and auctions for its compute capacity. Dion Harris, Nvidia’s senior director of high-performance computing and AI infrastructure, said his company is continuing to focus on improving AI efficiency in large part through software that, for example, helps choose appropriate models for particular tasks or improves memory management. “Nvidia has always added value to our hardware platform through our software,” Harris said, pointing to its open-source Nemotron models as one example. “We believe that a thriving AI ecosystem helps our broader go-to-market, so that’s really core to our strategy, and I think that will continue to be so.” — Tiffany Li Replit CEO Amjad Masad Replit CEO: OpenAI Price Cuts Slow Open Source AI Adoption AI coding startup Replit is using open source models in its own products and internally “probably less” now than it was in January, thanks to OpenAI aggressively slashing prices for its models, CEO Amjad Masad said. OpenAI earlier this week released GPT-6 Sol and Luna, the second- and third-most powerful versions of its latest models, with prices that were 50% below the same tiers of its previous model. Anthropic also released its Claude Opus 5.5, which the company said costs 40% less for customers to run than its prior top models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, while matching or beating its coding, reasoning and other features. The price cuts have big cost implications for ten-year-old Replit, which pays OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI providers when customers use its coding assistant to access their models to generate code. Replit also uses OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna model to power a feature that lets customers use its product to brainstorm new ideas for free. But open source models have their own unique challenges. Despite the flexibility they offer, open source models come with requirements that can add significantly to the expense of running them, according to Tamar Yehoshua, chief product and AI officer at Atlassian, which sells software that lets developers and other business teams collaborate on work. “There is a serving cost that is non-zero, and your overall cost can be sometimes hidden in [the] expertise that you need internally” to run open source models, Yehoshua said. — Kevin McLaughlin Alexander Embiricos, product lead for OpenAI’s enterprise products OpenAI: Customers Are Scratching Surface of AI OpenAI customers still aren’t tapping into all of the cutting-edge capabilities its models offer, said Alexander Embiricos, product lead for OpenAI’s enterprise products. “This is an amazingly powerful technology that we have, and we’re nowhere near the limit of how much value it can provide to us,” he said. “Even if models stop progressing like today, there is a bunch more product work that we can do.” Embiricos said OpenAI learns from customers how to shape its offerings, generally launching an open-ended AI product and seeing what sticks with users. From there, it can add features so it becomes easier to use, he said. This has been a particularly successful approach with customers of its $200-a-month Pro plan, which is used by individuals who often tap its coding or agentic functions at their jobs. “One of the best parts of working at OpenAI is we have this foot in consumer and this foot in enterprise,” he said. Though ChatGPT started as a consumer product, the past year OpenAI has been leaning heavily into selling its AI to businesses as competitor Anthropic’s coding tools and agents soared in popularity. Large companies are adopting some of OpenAI’s bleeding edge capabilities, such as coding agents, first because they have the most ambitious tasks—and the money to pay for advanced capabilities, said Embiricos. “We’re very early in the days of, like, we have these amazing agents that can do things, but we still need to let them do things and ask them to do things for us,” said Embiricos. He added: “We have to make it much easier to do that.” — Aaron Tilley Blackstone’s Jas Khaira Blackstone Could Eventually Buy AI Labs’ Debt Jas Khaira, head of Blackstone’s AI-focused investment team, said the firm is still figuring out which kinds of investors will step in to provide the massive amounts of financing needed for the AI buildout. The investment giant itself is waiting to see if debt from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic will be an attractive opportunity, he added. Blackstone is part of a venture that buys Google tensor processing units and then leases them out to AI developers . Khaira said “we’re going to look to upsize the scale of our purchases” given the compute shortage. Blackstone is also an investor through its credit and insurance arm. Khaira said that while Blackstone has mapped out the market’s needs for AI computing power, what kinds of debt investors would make the most sense for those needs is still evolving. “We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt,” he said, responding to an audience question about whether the cost of debt will have to rise in order to fund the build out. “We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from.” Khaira sketched out some high-level ideas, listing three buckets of financing he expects to play a role: public debt markets for investment grade companies, the private credit market, and debt issued by OpenAI and Anthropic once they go public. “A lot of that is going to depend on their ability to go public,” he said, “and their ability to be investment grade over time.” Khaira said Blackstone may also look to buy debt from the AI labs, at the right price. “But we’re also kind of waiting to see and evolve how that plays out,” he said, “both in terms of their activities and the pricing.” — Dakin Campbell Stephanie Cohen, Cloudflare Chief Strategy Officer. Block, Cloudflare Highlight the Potential and Pitfalls of AI-Driven Restructuring Top executives from Block and Cloudflare touted the benefits of AI-driven restructurings earlier this year that involved sweeping layoffs—but they also acknowledged the challenges they’ve encountered as a result. In February, Block cut its workforce by nearly half to reorient its staff for the AI era. It also has built a tool it calls Builderbot, an agent that can fix bugs in code or autonomously build as much as 80% of a new feature or product, said Owen Jennings, the financial-technology company’s business lead. One problem with the changes was a “massive proliferation” of code that needed to be properly vetted for mistakes or bugs—and the company didn’t have enough code reviewers to do that. “It became pretty clear the bottleneck was code review,” Jennings said. “Code review is even more important today than it was a year ago.” Cloudflare, where Stephanie Cohen is chief strategy officer, in May cut about 20% of its workforce. Incorporating AI into the company’s workflow has allowed the firm to drastically reduce the time for certain tasks, such as end-of-month financial presentations that used to take close to a week to produce. “It now takes them an hour,” Cohen said. But Cloudflare has also had to keep an eye on how staff are using AI, Cohen said. Employees in their go-to-market organization after the restructuring all tried to vibe-code the same kind of tool. “There was an enormous amount of wasted time,” Cohen said. Cloudflare has since set up meetings any staff can attend to learn how to use AI effectively. Surabhi Gupta, chief technology officer at Klaviyo, said employees experimenting with AI tools was a natural evolution of how the marketing software company works. Employees will come to work after a weekend and say, “look what I built,” Gupta said. She said the company strove to make sure what engineers were working on was connected to the best customer outcomes. –Michael Roddan Eric Zelikman, co-founder & CEO of humans& and Jerry Tworek, co-founder & CEO of Core Automation To Make Companies More Productive, AI Needs to Be More Reliable: Neolabs AI models are getting smarter in some domains such as advanced math problems and competitive programming tests, but they aren’t getting much more reliable at the tasks involved in most people’s jobs, said Jerry Tworek, chief executive of AI research startup Core Automation. As a result, people don’t trust AI agents to handle their jobs autonomously, he said. “If AI is so smart, why do we have to still come to work?” said Tworek, former vice president of research at OpenAI. “I would like to one day go on the beach and have models do my work for me. And I realized that to do it, I need a new algorithm.” Core Automation is researching such new algorithms, exploring designs of AI models that could prove to be more reliable than those used by the largest AI companies. A recent string of impressive results from the leading AI labs, including difficult math problems that OpenAI has solved, has led some researchers to believe that continuing with existing designs will result in AIs that exceed human performance on all tasks. The neolabs argue those existing designs have a long way to go. Customers are also currently limited in their ability to take advantage of AI products by the ability of employees to coordinate, share information and make decisions, said Eric Zelikman, co-founder and CEO at Humans&, a one-year old startup aiming to create AI that helps achieve users’ long-term goals. In contrast with Humans&’s approach, companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are in a “battle to the death” to automate as many of the specific tasks that people do as possible, such as coding, said Zelikman. Humans& stands out because it owns much of the hardware it uses to train its AI models. If the company had instead rented its two clusters of AI chips, it would have paid over $1 billion, said Zelikman, adding that the company is in the process of getting its third cluster ready. — Rocket Drew Left: Chris Dolan, Chief Data Center Officer at Crusoe. Right: Ricard Boada, Co-founder and CEO at Volta. How Leading AI Labs Can Earn Multiples of Their Annual Compute Costs As OpenAI and Anthropic race to secure more than $1 trillion of compute contracts—and are also trying to go public—it’s been unclear how much revenue they’re generating from these massive deals. One data point suggests it might be worth the investment. “The frontier AI labs are now monetizing compute at $75 million per megawatt a year compared to a levelized cost of compute of $15 million to $20 million,” said Ricard Boada, cofounder and CEO of Volta, a new company that secures access to financing, energy and compute capital for data centers. Potentially earning multiple times operating costs helps explain why the leading labs–which can command prices at the top of the market—are so eager to deploy power and chips, said Boada. Volta came out of stealth in August and said it signed a $10 billion dollar deal for compute in Norway with a frontier AI lab, reportedly Anthropic. Boada wouldn’t comment on specific customers, but said that the deal encompasses a $5 billion hardware purchase order and a $2 billion data center contract that Volta would have to finance. A gigawatt data center can cost as much as $15 billion to $20 billion in construction and another $30 billion to $40 billion in chips, said co-panelist Chris Dolan, Chief Data Center Officer of Crusoe. While a top frontier lab can potentially pay that off quickly, the payoff only comes if the developer can time the delivery of the power and compute together in a tightly orchestrated timeline. Some investors have been worried lately that public stock and debt investors could be more reluctant to finance the AI buildout. Boada and Dolan said that AI data center contracts can generate predictable returns as the industry matures, but that capital providers are growing more choosy about whom to back. “The capital markets are catching up to this new asset class,” Dolan said. — Phoebe Liu

title: Google Nears Release of Flagship Gemini 4 AI Model
content: Google is nearing the release of its newest flagship model, Gemini 4, the head of its DeepMind division said Wednesday, a long-awaited development after the tech giant fell behind rivals Anthropic and OpenAI in the AI model race. Speaking at The Information’s AI Agenda Live Summit, in his first media appearance as the new leader of Google DeepMind, Koray Kavukcuoglu said Gemini 4 is in the early days of a phase of development called post-training, in which a base AI model is refined to behave reliably. He said he hopes the model will be released “much earlier” than the end of the year. “Our intention is to, like—as soon as possible—to release an early post-training output because we see the results and we are excited,” he said, in conversation with The Information’s editor-in-chief Jessica Lessin. Then, Google would “continue the fast-paced iterations.” Gemini 4 would be Google’s first next-generation flagship model since the launch of the Gemini 3 line late last year—though it released an update, Gemini 3.1, in February and has released a series of smaller, cheaper Flash models less capable of complex reasoning. Google CEO Sundar Pichai had said in May at the company’s annual I/O conference that it would release a major update, Gemini 3.5 Pro, in June, but the release never came. Kavukcuoglu said that instead of releasing Gemini 3.5 Pro, the company “took a little bit of a step back” after the release of Gemini models 3 and 3.1 and focused on introducing the Flash models. “For us, what was important is to maximize the speed of learning at the time,” he said. He didn’t specify whether Google has officially scrapped Gemini 3.5 Pro, but made clear its focus is releasing Gemini 4. Rival Anthropic this spring launched its powerful new Mythos family of models, which it upgraded this month, and OpenAI started launching its similarly capable GPT-6 models in early September. Both are more capable than Google’s most advanced current models. Asked Wednesday whether he worries that Google has fallen behind peers, Kavukcuoglu said he’s “a hundred percent confident” in his team. “We have [an] insanely strong team, and I have the utmost trust in the team,” he said. “In my mind, it’s a certainty that we are always gonna be at the frontier.” Kavukcuoglu said Google is in the middle of developing guardrails and safety testing for Gemini 4, which is being used internally by engineers to run its Antigravity AI coding tool. Kavukcuoglu took the helm of Google’s AI business in August, transitioning to senior vice president of Google DeepMind from chief technology officer, after Demis Hassabis left his role as Google DeepMind CEO to be chairman of the unit and chief scientist of Google parent Alphabet. Kavukcuoglu is also the chief AI architect of Google. Google has caught up from a lagging position in the AI model race before. Its Gemini 3 model was such a leap that it prompted OpenAI to declare a “code red” effort to catch up to the search giant. Unlike his peers in the AI industry, Kavukcuoglu said doesn’t have a strong opinion about whether or not the industry has achieved AGI, or artificial general intelligence, generally defined as AI that equals or exceeds human abilities across all tasks. “The conversation of [whether] we achieved AGI or not is not the right conversation,” he said. “The conversation is more about are we able to build intelligent agents that we can trust?” Kavukcuoglu said Google’s frontier model developments will also help the tech giant advance its rapidly growing hardware business, in which it produces AI chips called TPUs, or tensor processing units. The company this year began selling TPUs to customers, rather than solely selling access to the hardware through its cloud business, as it steps up competition with Nvidia . Kavukcuoglu said that Google DeepMind’s work on new models gives its hardware engineers visibility into how it will design its “next two or three generations” of chips.

title: Amazon’s New AI Offer Reflects Discounting Surge
content: Have we gone full circle on AI pricing? A bunch of tech firms are throwing around discounts and free offers for AI products, with Amazon on Wednesday announcing that merchants selling on its shopping site will get a year’s free use of its Quick Plus AI assistant product. Microsoft, meanwhile, is discounting Copilot AI subscriptions heavily, we reported Tuesday night . Both offers are part of a wave of discounting by various software firms and AI labs such as OpenAI. We keep hearing from tech executives about the transformative nature of AI. And yet there’s clearly some resistance among businesses to paying full price for it, which seems a bit of an issue given how much money it is costing to build out the infrastructure for running AI on a mass scale. Something has to give. As Apollo Global Management’s chief economist, Torsten Slok, noted in his daily email on Monday, credit investors are buying bonds of the hyperscalers—a reference to cloud firms—right now on the assumption that their operating cash flow will triple between 2025 and 2030. “If this doesn’t happen, then the risk is that the AI trade weakens, with credit spreads widening, capex plans getting cut,” Slok wrote. The current pricing environment is reminiscent of the early days of the AI revolution, two or three years ago, when AI companies were trying to persuade people to try their products and bringing in revenue was an afterthought. In 2024, for instance , OpenAI, Anthropic and Google slashed the price of their flagship models by more than 90%. But that trend reversed last year, as companies focused more on recouping their investments. Enterprise software firms followed suit, shifting to usage-based pricing from charging people based on the number of people using AI. That seat-based model had proved to be a money-loser when employees began ratcheting up their use of AI. But as we said in April , customers have complained that they pay more in the usage-based model—which is why we find ourselves back in a world of discounting. It’s a similar issue in the consumer market: As former Apple and Nest executive Tony Fadell said in an X post on Wednesday, “What consumers want is for AI to be useful, easy to access, and FREE or bundled into something they already pay for.” To be sure, some of the discounts now offered aim to drive up customer spending in different ways. Microsoft, for instance, still offers seat-based pricing accompanied by pay-as-you-go features that add a usage component. It is now discounting the seat costs in the hope that selling subscriptions for more employees will drive usage-based bills higher. You have to imagine the customers will eventually figure that out. One way to solve this mess is to reduce the number of firms clamoring for a piece of the AI action. Right now we’ve got older software firms trying to remake themselves with AI products, alongside startups and AI firms offering similar products. The established software firms, mostly public companies, have to demonstrate revenue growth—no matter how slow—even though that’s probably not realistic. Their business customers will likely argue they want AI to displace some of their existing software bills rather than pay more overall. A shakeout is coming. Cutting prices for a product as expensive as AI isn’t sustainable. OpenAI’s Hack Down Under OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was neatly turned out in a suit and tie when he spoke to the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday afternoon—in person, unlike Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who spoke to the body by Zoom. Altman needs to be on his best behavior, given the antics OpenAI agents have been up to lately. For instance, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters in New York that an OpenAI agent had broken into one of his country’s government websites, accessing both public and nonpublic files. It was the latest in a series of episodes involving AI agents from various firms breaking into outside computer systems. You have to wonder: How do these agents decide who to hack? In Other News • Chinese AI researchers have increasingly opted to stay and work in their home country, leading China to become the top destination for elite AI talent, according to a study by think tank Carnegie China. The research found that the share of top AI researchers working in China rose from 27.1% in 2022 to 40.6% in 2025. The share of AI talent in the U.S. fell from 46.4% to 34.2% over the same period. • Kevin Salimian, former managing director at investment firm Lone Pine Capital, has launched a new firm with more than $500 million in committed capital , The Information reported. • OpenAI and Grab, a Singapore-based transport and food-delivery company, on Wednesday launched a program to train Grab’s drivers, merchants and delivery riders to use ChatGPT for work. • Anthropic said Claude helped discover a previously unknown molecular system that the company said could represent a new gene-editing tool akin to CRISPR, which has transformed the creation of new gene therapies. • OpenAI has hired Patreon co-founder Sam Yam to lead a new creator product division, Creator Product, Yam announced Wednesday on X , a sign of the company’s renewed interest in attracting consumers. • Jas Khaira, head of Blackstone’s AI-focused investment team, said on Wednesday that the firm is still figuring out which kinds of investors will step in to provide the massive amounts of financing still needed for the AI buildout. The investment giant itself is waiting to see if debt from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic will be an attractive opportunity, he added. More here. title: Exclusive: GM Is Pumping Out Cathodes And Moving to Bypass China's Battery Chokehold
content: Over the last year, researchers working in a sprawling General Motors lab in Warren, Mich., prepared 18 variations of a new battery chemistry designed to reduce a battery’s cost, one of the biggest obstacles to greater U.S. consumer interest in electric vehicles. GM bosses believed that if they landed on the right formulation for this unusual battery, powered by cheap manganese, the company would finally have a chance, after numerous false starts, to launch affordable EVs that would sell in droves. After much debate, GM winnowed down the list to a single formulation, and late last month workers began slathering the concoction on long, wide sheets of ultrathin aluminum foil and pumping out cathodes at a large new testing factory adjacent to the Warren lab. Assuming the company successfully scales up production in these tests, it plans to deploy the manganese batteries in at least one new commercial EV in 2028 and more in the years after. The startup of the testing facility and the initial production of cathodes, reported here for the first time, mark a key new stage in a methodical attempt by GM to move gingerly back into EVs after writing down $6 billion in EV investments just eight months ago. In 2024 and 2025, GM also wrote down around $1.1 billion in investments in Cruise, the autonomous driving subsidiary it shut down in late 2024. In embracing the manganese battery, GM is attempting to bypass China’s stranglehold on the world’s battery and EV industries. The manganese battery—actually a mixture of manganese with some lithium and nickel—is one of two new types of cheap batteries that GM intends to produce in future years at gigawatt scale. GM chose the two in large part because China does not control the output of either. That wasn’t the only reason, however. GM also chose the manganese battery, known as lithium manganese rich, or LMR, because it packs more energy than China’s primary EV battery, lithium iron phosphate, but can be made more cheaply, said Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability. No major Chinese company makes LMR batteries. The other battery chemistry that GM intends to make is sodium-ion, which is based on ultracheap soda ash. Multiple Chinese companies make sodium-ion batteries at large scale, but since it is a relatively new chemistry, GM believes there is still time for other players to get in on the game. In other words, GM’s new EV strategy is all about making inexpensive electric cars, but it’s also about distancing itself from China and countering the country’s ability to choke off the supplies the company needs to make those cars. Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington this week, for instance, Beijing cut its exports of rare earth magnets to the U.S. by 21% as if to remind the U.S. of the leverage it wields. China supplies roughly 90% of the world’s rare earth magnets, which are essential in EV motors (as well as robots, drones, weapons, portable electronics and medical devices). Analysts expect President Donald Trump to raise the subject of the cutoff with Xi. China has also restricted exports of its best LFP and the equipment needed to make it. As GM gets into battery making in a big way, it is attempting to eliminate pitfalls that have tripped up and killed off other companies. Dozens of U.S. battery startups have shut down in the last several years after attempting to jump too quickly to full commercial production; others have simply decided not to attempt making batteries at all and are instead trying to license their components to others. This is because new battery chemistries frequently work really well in the lab but then go haywire during the attempt to produce them at factory scale: The electrode slurry often does not lay down uniformly, flaws emerge in the aluminum or copper foils, or the battery layers do not align precisely, as they must to avoid a failure. The difficulty with making batteries at high volume is why only a few speciality companies—mostly Chinese—dominate the industry. Just two companies—China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd. and BYD—make more than half the world’s lithium-ion batteries. No major Western car company apart from Tesla has successfully turned itself into a battery manufacturer. Volkswagen has tried but has not yet succeeded, and even Tesla continues to do so only at a relatively small scale. GM’s battery testing facility, the Battery Cell Development Center, is the company’s attempt to tackle the manufacturing hurdle—a middle step between pilot scale production and planned gigawatt-scale commercial manufacturing. The $900 million battery-making complex consists of three large buildings built adjacent to one another. Company researchers make and test dozens of chemistries at the research lab. They then send the promising ones next door to a pilot manufacturing facility, which has small production lines that can make around 50 battery cells per month. From there, the ones GM intends to scale up into commercial batteries will go to the BCDC, which will be able to pump out thousands of test cells a month, the company said. There, GM can work the high-production kinks out of new technologies like LMR and sodium ion before they move to full commercialization at plants outside its premises. (Full-scale production is typically in the tens of millions of cells a month.) Other companies have failed because they have skipped this middle step and moved directly to full-scale manufacturing from pilot-scale production, said Mo Gallegos, director of the BCDC. Doing so has been “just a recipe for disaster, as we’ve kind of seen before,” he said. “So this, the BCDC, was the missing tool. We invested in this piece to be able to industrialize learnings and implement those so that we can actually have success in scaling new chemistries through our whole ecosystem.” GM declined to say when it would begin to develop sodium-ion cells, which operate similarly to lithium-ion batteries but replace the lithium with sodium. Sodium-ion batteries are significantly less energy dense than lithium-ion ones, and almost no EV makers plan to use them in cars. However, GM intends to commercialize sodium-ion batteries for use on the grid and to power AI data centers. In June, the company announced that it would develop sodium-ion batteries with Peak Energy, a Colorado battery startup that currently buys sodium-ion batteries in China and elsewhere in Asia, then packages them into stationary storage systems. GM and Peak plan to develop a next-generation sodium-ion battery that will use no Chinese materials. They will test production of that battery at BCDC. “We can figure out how to make the cells, design our own cells, or to drive down the cost further and improve the performance,” said Kelty. GM’s renewed effort to tackle EVs mirrors Ford’s similar attempt from another angle: On the same 2028 timeline as that of GM’s new LMR battery, Ford intends to release the Fathom, a midsize electric pickup that it also claims will directly confront the Chinese juggernaut. The twin efforts reflect the U.S.’s attempt to compete in a new age in which China and its turbocharged economy are the vanguard. On one hand, a leading car-industry lobbying group argued last week that the U.S. should never under any circumstances allow Chinese cars into the U.S. On the other, GM and Ford appear to realize that a total blockade is probably unrealistic and that they are eventually going to have to compete with Chinese car companies at home.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program
Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced plans to introduce legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along the country’s southern border.
The announcement comes just days after publication of an MIT Technology Review investigation, “Dying on Camera,” which looked at deaths near these towers. Nearly one in four deaths we analyzed between 2015 and early 2026 occurred within their advertised range.
Ramirez, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee, cited our reporting that nearly “1,100 people have died within range of a billion-dollar surveillance tower system between 2015 and 2026,” adding, “The towers that we have paid a billion dollars to just don’t work.”
Here’s what she’s proposing and what it could mean for the border surveillance program.
—Eileen Guo
Read all of MIT Technology Review’s groundbreaking “virtual wall” investigation here.
Roundtables: the deadly failures of the virtual border wall
The US spent billions building the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border, promising they will help detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives. But MIT Technology Review has documented more than a thousand people who moved through areas watched by these towers without being caught—and ultimately died there.
Next Monday, join our editor-in-chief Mat Honan, senior AI reporter James O’Donnell, and senior reporter for features and investigations Eileen Guo for a subscriber-only conversation about the investigation. They’ll examine the failures of border surveillance technology and uncover the stories of the people who die in the borderlands.

If ever a blade of grass grew on Mars, those days are over. But could they begin again? What would it take to grow plants to feed future astronauts on Mars?

title: AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week
content:
AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week
The debate is louder than usual as climate voices gather.
This week, world leaders descended on Manhattan for the UN General Assembly. It’s also New York Climate Week—investors, policymakers, advocates, and journalists are colliding at panels, talks, and fancy dinners.
With so many climate voices in one place, the discourse can feel a little louder than usual. This year, the unavoidable topic is artificial intelligence.
There’s been a growing tension bubbling up about AI’s impacts on climate and climate tech. Depending on where you stand, you might point to AI’s potential for advancing research, or to the way funding and attention from Big Tech is trickling into energy startups. Or you might focus on the emissions-heavy natural-gas buildout that’s unfolding to meet the sector’s electricity demand.
Everyone seems to agree that AI is important. The big question for those in the climate world, and the conversation I’m constantly having and hearing this week, involves how you see its influence unfolding.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres highlighted the AI and climate crossover in a speech on the first day of the assembly. “The climate crisis fuels instability and displacement,” Guterres said. “Artificial intelligence could help solve all these challenges, or it could make them worse.”
It feels relevant that this year is the first that the world has really had to grapple with the fact that climate goals are slipping out of reach. A recent report from the UN Environment Program said that the world has nearly passed the point where we could possibly keep warming to less than 1.5 °C above preindustrial levels.
Since we’ve essentially missed this target, the report lays out the need not only to quickly and drastically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, but also to employ carbon removal to help suck up emissions that have already been released into the atmosphere.
The billion-dollar question is whether AI could help with any of this.
The energy-intensive technology is certainly shining a spotlight on the need to build out electricity supplies and shore up grid reliability. The result is more attention and money for energy technologies, some of which happen to be low- or zero-emissions.
As I’ve covered before, startups across the energy and climate sectors are benefiting. Firms in nuclear, geothermal, wind, and solar power have signed deals with the likes of Google, Meta, and others looking to power their new or growing data centers.
Global climate-tech investment from venture capital hit $26 billion in the first half of 2026, according to data from Currence, a finance tracker for the industry. That’s 55% higher than last year, and products and services for data centers are getting a massive slice of that pie.
But as a Semafor piece about the report points out, some sectors are slipping through the cracks: Carbon management and low-carbon fuels saw VC investment plummet this year. These are important solutions for addressing climate change but may not be able to sell themselves to a data center.
So far, the data center buildout has come with a hefty emissions toll. A few years ago, Microsoft, Google, and Meta all had ambitious goals to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions. Now they’ve all seen emissions rise, largely because of data centers that are needed to power AI.
Some people are optimistic. AI could help speed up progress in areas like the search for new catalysts, as Evelyn Wang, MIT’s VP of energy and climate, pointed out during a panel. And data centers won’t add to climate and water problems forever, Wang told the Associated Press. (She puts the timeline at about a decade until data centers no longer add to planet-warming emissions.)
But a whole lot of natural gas is coming online to meet the immediate demand created by new data centers. And once those power plants are built, they have a decades-long lifetime.
That’s partly why public pushback to AI is growing—people are seeing more pollution and noise near these data centers and the power plants that provide them with electricity. Overall, what I’m hearing this week is that many in the climate sector are skeptical of AI, at best.
“AI leaders are now on thin ice when it comes to license to operate and sinking deep underwater when it comes to public support,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell in a speech this week. “Tech titans need to start showing why the benefits of AI outweigh its skyrocketing costs—for the many, not just the tiny few.”

Das Fraunhofer Heinrich-Hertz-Institut (HHI) freut sich über die Bekanntgabe des IEEE Arun N. Netravali Video Analytics, Technology, and Systems Award 2027, der an Benjamin Bross (Fraunhofer HHI), Jens-Rainer Ohm (RWTH Aachen) und Gary J. Sullivan (Dolby Laboratories) verliehen wird. Mit dieser Auszeichnung werden die führende Rolle der drei Preisträger bei der Standardisierung der Videokodierung sowie die Bedeutung des Standards gewürdigt, den sie gemeinsam mit der Videoindustrie erfolgreich entwickelt haben.
IEEE würdigt drei Schlüsselpersonen der HEVC-Standardisierung
Benjamin Bross, Leiter der Forschungsgruppe Videokodierungssysteme am Fraunhofer HHI, Prof. Dr.-Ing. Jens-Rainer Ohm, emeritierter Professor und ehemaliger Leiter des Instituts für Nachrichtentechnik an der RWTH Aachen, sowie Dr. Gary J. Sullivan, Director of Video Research & Standards bei Dolby Laboratories, wurden vom Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), der weltweit größten technischen Fachorganisation und gemeinnützigen Einrichtung zur Förderung von Technologien zum Nutzen der Menschheit, als Preisträger bekannt gegeben.
Die Auszeichnung wurde ihnen „für ihre Führungsrolle und ihre Beiträge zur Entwicklung des internationalen Standards High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC)“ verliehen.
Führende Rolle bei der Entwicklung eines wegweisenden Videostandards
Die Entwicklung des HEVC-Standards brachte weltweit führende Experten und Expertinnen der Internationalen Fernmeldeunion (ITU), der Internationalen Organisation für Normung (ISO) und der Internationalen Elektrotechnischen Kommission (IEC) in einem Team namens „Joint Collaborative Team on Video Coding“ (JCT-VC) zusammen. Prof. Ohm und Dr. Sullivan leiteten die Entwicklung des Standards, und Benjamin Bross war der leitende Redakteur des Spezifikationsdokuments. Gemeinsam koordinierten und lenkten sie einen Prozess, in dessen Rahmen Tausende technischer Beitragsdokumente von rund tausend technischen Experten und Expertinnen aus der internationalen Fachgemeinschaft analysiert wurden. Dabei wurden die technischen Eigenschaften des Standards innerhalb des JCT-VC im Konsens ausgewählt und weiter verfeinert. Ihre Federführung stellte sicher, dass der Standard für eine Umsetzung im Massenmarkt praxistauglich war und zugleich vollständig und detailliert technisch spezifiziert wurde.
Der HEVC-Standard, auch bekannt als H.265 und MPEG-H Part 2, stellt einen bedeutenden Fortschritt gegenüber seinem Vorgänger dar, dem zehn Jahre zuvor entwickelten und etablierten AVC-Standard. HEVC ermöglicht eine Reduzierung der für die Videokodierung erforderlichen Bitrate um etwa 50 % bei gleicher Bildqualität wie bei AVC. Nach koordinierten Forschungsarbeiten von Experten aus ITU-T- und ISO/IEC-Arbeitsgruppen wurde 2010 das JCT-VC gegründet, das intensiv an der Konzeption und Spezifikation des HEVC-Standards arbeitete und 2013 die erste Version fertigstellte. Der Standard wurde von der Industrie rasch übernommen. Er trug maßgeblich zur erfolgreichen Einführung mehrerer weiterer bedeutender Fortschritte in der Videotechnologie bei, darunter Ultra-High-Definition-Auflösung (UHD), 10-Bit-Videopräzision, High Dynamic Range (HDR) mit breitem Farbraum (WCG), hohe Bildraten und Video-Streaming-Dienste. Bis Ende 2015 unterstützten die meisten neuen PCs und Mobilgeräte sowie praktisch alle 4K-UHD-Fernseher bereits den bahnbrechenden HEVC-Standard.
HEVC verändert Videokompression und -übertragung
Die Geschichte der Standardisierung der Videokompression war bislang von Bestrebungen zur Maximierung der Kompressionsleistung geprägt. Als die Entwicklung von HEVC begann, führten eine zunehmende Vielfalt an Diensten, die wachsende Beliebtheit von HD-Video selbst in mobilen Anwendungen sowie die aufkommenden Formate jenseits von HD (z. B. 4K×2K-Auflösung) zu einem noch stärkeren Bedarf an verbesserter Kompressionsleistung. HEVC wurde so konzipiert, dass es im Wesentlichen alle bestehenden Anwendungen früherer Standards abdeckt, wobei der Schwerpunkt insbesondere auf zwei Schlüsselthemen lag: der erhöhten Videoauflösung und dem verstärkten Einsatz paralleler Verarbeitungsarchitekturen. Zwar ist HEVC das Ergebnis einer gemeinsamen Entwicklung durch ein großes Expertenteam, doch ist es die herausragende Leistung der Projektleiter und des Chefredakteurs, die Entwicklung des resultierenden Standards in die von der Industrie benötigte Richtung zu lenken und dabei auf die Verarbeitungsfähigkeit von Echtzeitsystemen abzustimmen.
Von weltweiter Ausstrahlung bis zum Streaming jenseits der Erde
Der HEVC-Standard hat sich in mehreren Ländern, darunter Deutschland, Italien, den Niederlanden, Polen, Kroatien und der Tschechischen Republik, zum primären Videoübertragungsformat entwickelt. Er wurde neben den Spezifikationen der ITU, ISO und IEC auch in die Branchenspezifikationen vieler anderer Organisationen übernommen, darunter 3GPP, die 8K Association, ANSI/SCTE, ARIB, ATSC, BD ROM, CTA/CEA, Digital UK, ETSI/DVB, ETSI/EBU, IETF, NATO, MISB und das Ultra HD Forum. Decoder mit geringem Stromverbrauch sind bei praktisch allen Herstellern von Videochips erhältlich, und die Codierung wird in nahezu allen professionellen Videoproduktions-Workflows unterstützt. Die NASA gab im März 2026 sogar bekannt, dass ihr Streaming-Dienst „NASA+“ HEVC nutze, darunter auch für das Videomaterial zur bemannten Artemis-II-Mission jenseits der Mondumlaufbahn, wodurch der Standard nicht nur weltweit, sondern auch im Weltraum zum Einsatz kommt.
Ein Standard mit nachhaltiger globaler Wirkung
HEVC wird mittlerweile von mehr als 90 % der derzeit hergestellten Fernseher, PCs, Mobiltelefone und Webbrowser unterstützt und findet breite Anwendung bei Streaming-Anbietern, Fernsehsendern, Videoaufzeichnungsgeräten und Videoüberwachungs-systemen. Die Entwicklung des HEVC-Standards wurde 2017 erstmals mit einem Primetime Engineering Emmy Award für das JCT-VC ausgezeichnet. Ende 2023 schätzte Futuresource Consulting, dass „über 96 % der heute verkauften Videoprodukte für Endverbraucher über eine HEVC-Wiedergabefunktion verfügen, was jährlich insgesamt 2,3 Milliarden Endgeräten entspricht; und diese Zahl steigt von Jahr zu Jahr“. Die enorme Bedeutung effizienter Videokompressionstechnologie wird deutlich, wenn man bedenkt, dass etwa 80 % des Datenverkehrs in den weltweiten Kommunikationsnetzen mittlerweile aus Videodaten besteht. Im April 2026 berichtete NETINT, dass der Anteil der Videofachleute, die HEVC nutzen oder dessen baldigen Einsatz planen, sich der Sättigungsgrenze nähert und damit den Anteil jedes anderen Videoformats übertroffen hat.
Das Fraunhofer HHI gratuliert Benjamin Bross, Jens-Rainer Ohm und Gary J. Sullivan zu dieser Anerkennung durch das IEEE, die die globale Bedeutung des HEVC-Standards unterstreicht.
